clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a list of numbers and a target value, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target exactly. Assume exactly one valid pair exists, and the same element can't be used twice.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: The merchant wants exactly 600,000 Berries for the map piece — not a coin more, not a coin less — and he only accepts TWO chests at once!

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: There are only three chests here, so we could just try every pair by hand... but that gets ugly fast if there are hundreds of them.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then let's not check every pair. I'll remember every chest we've already opened — and for each new one, I only need to ask: 'have I already seen the amount that completes it?'

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Chest one: 300,000. I need 300,000 more to reach the target — nothing in my notes yet. I'll log it and move on.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Chest two: 200,000. I need 400,000 more — still nothing logged that matches. Log this one too.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Chest three: 400,000. I need 200,000 more to complete it — and that's already in my notes, from chest two!

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Chest two and chest three — 200,000 plus 400,000 is exactly 600,000. That's the pair.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! And you never even touched chest one again! Meat time!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That's the whole trick: check the notes before you write anything new down, and you only ever look at each chest once. One pass, one pair — never re-comparing chests against each other directly.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Log the current chest AFTER checking for its complement, not before — otherwise a target that is exactly double one value (e.g. target=6, chest=3) would incorrectly pair a chest with itself.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Two non-negative integers are stored as linked lists with their digits in reverse order. Add them and return the sum as a linked list in the same form.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The Skypiean bells record numbers backwards — the smallest place first. Two of them have to be added, and the answer written the same way.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Backwards is a gift, not an obstacle. Column addition starts at the smallest place, and these lists already begin there — so we simply walk both from the head, adding as we go.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Two plus five is seven. Four plus six is ten — write zero, carry one. Three plus four plus the carry is eight.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And the lists needn't be the same length. A missing digit is just a zero.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So the loop runs while either list has nodes left OR a carry is outstanding — the same three-condition loop as adding binary strings. A final carry becomes a new node at the end.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: A dummy head makes building the answer painless. Otherwise the first node needs its own special case, separate from all the rest.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Attach to the dummy's tail every time, and return the dummy's next at the end. One shape for every node, first included.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: What if the bells were recorded the normal way round, biggest place first?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then you would reverse both lists, add, and reverse the answer — or push the digits onto stacks and pop them. Either way you are paying to get back to the order this problem hands you for free.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Ending the loop when both lists are exhausted and dropping a final carry, so 5 + 5 returns a single node 0 instead of 0 → 1. And forgetting that the lists may differ in length.

3.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
3.epTitle: Bink's Sake, Never Twice in a Row

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a string, find the length of the longest contiguous substring in which no character repeats.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: Fifty years alone on the Rumbar's deck, and I only had this much of the melody left in my head — I promised Laboon I'd play the whole thing someday. Yohoho.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: But some of the notes repeat! If I hum a note twice in the same phrase it sounds muddy — you said so yourself. What's the LONGEST clean run in here, with no note repeated?

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: First note: B. A phrase of one, and it's clean so far.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: I, then N, then K — none of them repeat anything still ringing in the phrase. The window just keeps growing to the right.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Next note's a B again — and we already have one ringing, back at the start of the phrase!

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: So the phrase can no longer start before the note right after that old B. Drop it from the front — the window's left edge jumps forward, not one note at a time, straight to where it needs to be.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: Last note: S. Nothing in the current phrase repeats it — the window grows again, and this is the longest clean run yet.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Five notes, never checking a note twice against the whole phrase — just remembering the last place you saw each one. That's amazing, Brook!

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Shrinking the window one note at a time from the left instead of jumping the left edge directly to (last seen index of the repeat) + 1 — it still works, but throws away the O(1)-per-step jump that makes the single-pass argument clean.

4.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
4.epTitle: The Cut That Balances Two Ledgers

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given two sorted arrays, return the median of their combined elements. The overall run time must be O(log(m + n)).

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Two ledgers, each already in order, and we need the middle value of the two combined — without combining them, because they've asked for logarithmic time.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Merging them is linear and easy. Logarithmic in the total means we can't even LOOK at every entry.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then stop thinking about the median as a value and think of it as a CUT. We need to split the combined ledger into a left half and a right half of equal size, where everything on the left is at most everything on the right.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And each ledger gets exactly one cut. So if I choose how many entries to take from A, the number from B is forced — the halves must add to half the total.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One free choice, and it is what we binary search over. Not the values — the position of the cut in the smaller ledger.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: How do I know a cut is the right one?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Check the four entries either side of the two cuts. The cut is correct when A's last-taken is at most B's first-untaken, and B's last-taken is at most A's first-untaken. Otherwise you have taken too many from one side and you move the cut.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Then the median is either the largest on the left, or the average of that and the smallest on the right, depending on whether the total is odd or even.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Always binary search the SMALLER ledger — it bounds the number of steps and keeps the index arithmetic in range. And treat a cut at either end as plus or minus infinity, so the empty side never needs a special case.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Infinities instead of edge cases. That turns four awkward branches into no branches at all.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Searching the larger array, which lets the derived index fall out of range. And handling the empty-side cases by hand instead of using ±infinity sentinels, which is where most implementations break.

5.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
5.epTitle: The Longest Line That Reads Both Ways

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a string, return the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The last poneglyph carries one line that reads identically in both directions. We need the longest such run in the inscription.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Check every substring and test each one? That's every start and end, times the cost of checking. Cubic.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Two better ways. The table version says a run is a palindrome when its ends match and the run inside it is one too — that is a two-dimensional DP over start and end.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Quadratic time and quadratic space. What's the other way?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Grow from the centre. Every palindrome has one, so stand at each position and push outward while the two sides agree.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: But 'aba' has a centre ON a letter, and 'abba' has a centre BETWEEN two letters. Those aren't the same kind of position.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is why there are two centres per position — one on the character, one in the gap after it. Roughly two n centres in total, and missing the even case is the classic bug here.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Quadratic time still, but constant space. And far easier to write than the table.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is a linear algorithm — Manacher's — and it is worth being able to name. But expand-around-centre is the one to write, and the one they expect.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Only considering odd-length centres, which misses "abba" entirely. Also, the expansion must stop at the string bounds, not merely on a mismatch.

6.title: Zigzag Conversion
6.epTitle: The Message Written Down the Mast

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Write a string in a zigzag pattern across a given number of rows, then read it off row by row.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The message runs down the mast, then diagonally back up, then down again — and to read it you take each crossbar in turn, left to right.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Do we have to build the whole grid? Most of it would be empty.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: No grid at all. Keep one bucket per row and walk the message once, appending each character to the row you are currently on.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And the row index just goes down, down, down, then up, up, up.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Carry a direction of plus one or minus one, and flip it whenever you reach the top row or the bottom row. That single flip is the entire zigzag.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Then concatenate the buckets in order and you have the answer. Linear time, and only the characters themselves are stored.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: What if there's only one row? Then there's no zigzag at all.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The direction would flip on every character and the index would try to leave the mast. So guard it: one row, or a row count at least the message length, means the answer is the message unchanged.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: The numRows = 1 case, where the direction flips every step and the row index escapes the range. Also, building the two-dimensional grid explicitly, which wastes space on cells that are never used.

9.title: Palindrome Number
9.epTitle: The Drum Beat That Mirrors Itself

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Determine whether an integer reads the same forwards and backwards, without converting it to a string.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Kaido's war drums beat a number, and the signal only counts if it mirrors itself. No writing it down as text — we have to work with the number as a number.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Reverse the whole thing and compare? But reversing a large number can overflow before you get to compare it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So reverse only HALF of it. Peel digits off the back and build them up until the built half is at least as large as what remains at the front — that is the midpoint.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: 121: peel the 1, leaving 12 against 1. Peel the 2, leaving 1 against 12. Now the built half is larger, so we've passed the middle.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: For an odd number of digits the middle digit sits alone in the built half, so drop it with a division by ten before comparing. Both cases handled with one extra comparison.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: What about negatives? Minus one two one reversed reads one two one minus.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Never a palindrome — the sign only ever sits at the front. Reject anything negative immediately.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And ten? Reversed that's one, which isn't ten. The trailing zero is the problem — nothing but zero itself may end in zero.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Both of those are cheap guards at the top, and both are cases a lazy test set will miss. Half-reversal never overflows, and the whole thing runs in half the digits.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Reversing the whole number, which can overflow in a fixed-width language before the comparison happens. And missing the two guards: negatives are never palindromes, and any non-zero number ending in 0 cannot be one.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of non-negative integers where each value is the height of a vertical line at that index, choose two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container. The container holds water up to width (the distance between the two lines) times height (the shorter of the two line heights) — find the maximum amount of water any pair of lines can hold.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Nine stone pillars, all different heights. Wall off two of them and the gap between holds rainwater — but only up to whichever pillar is SHORTER. Height above that just spills over the top.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Checking every pair by hand is thirty-six comparisons for just nine pillars. That's not a plan, that's a chore.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Is there a way to skip pairs without even looking at them?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Start at the two outer pillars — the widest gap there is. Whichever one is shorter is the bottleneck. Moving the TALLER pillar's pointer inward only shrinks the width and can never raise that bottleneck, so it can never help. Only stepping the SHORTER pillar inward has any chance of finding something taller. That's the only move we ever make.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Pillar 0 is height 1, pillar 8 is height 7. Width eight, bottleneck height one — eight units of water. The left pillar is shorter, so it steps in.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Pillar 1 is height 8, pillar 8 is still height 7. Width seven, bottleneck height seven — forty-nine! Now the RIGHT pillar is the shorter one, so it steps in next.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: From here the gap only keeps narrowing — pillar 8 down to 7, then 6, then 5, then 4, then 3, then 2 — and none of those widths, even against pillar 1's wall of eight, can multiply back up to forty-nine.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So the two walls just keep marching toward each other until they meet, and whatever the biggest number we wrote down was — that stays the answer?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Exactly. Once the pointers meet, we stop. Best area found: forty-nine, between pillar 1 and pillar 8.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: One pass. Never move the tall one.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Moving the taller pointer (or both pointers) instead of always moving the shorter one. Moving the taller side can only shrink the width while the bottleneck height stays capped by the same short pillar (or gets worse), so it can silently step past the true optimal pair.

12.title: Integer to Roman
12.epTitle: Carving the Number Back Into Stone

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Convert an integer to a Roman numeral, using the subtractive forms where they apply.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Now the other direction — carve nineteen ninety-four into the stone the old way. And the subtractive pairs have to come out right.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Do we handle the digits one at a time, with a special case whenever a digit is four or nine?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is a tidier way. Put the six subtractive forms into the value table as first-class entries — nine hundred is CM, four is IV — and then simply take the largest that fits, repeatedly.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So no special cases at all. Nineteen ninety-four: M leaves nine ninety-four. CM leaves ninety-four. XC leaves four. IV leaves nothing.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Why is the greedy safe? Greedy algorithms usually need an argument.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Because this particular set of values is designed so that taking the largest that fits is always optimal — it is a canonical system. The same greedy on an arbitrary coin set would be wrong.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So the correctness comes from the value set, not from the algorithm. Good to know which is doing the work.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And note the asymmetry with reading numerals. Parsing is cleanest with the comparison RULE; generating is cleanest with the six forms ENUMERATED. Opposite choices, same notation.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Handling each decimal digit with a branch for 4 and 9, which is longer and error-prone. And assuming the greedy is generally safe — it is correct here because the Roman value set is canonical, not because greedy always works on coin-like problems.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Convert a Roman numeral string to an integer. A smaller value placed before a larger one is subtracted rather than added.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The Old Kingdom carved its numbers as letters, largest first — except where a smaller letter sits before a larger one, and then it is subtracted.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So we need to spot the six special pairs — IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, CM — and handle them separately?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: You can, but there is a rule that needs no list at all. Walk the letters and compare each to the one after it. If it is smaller, subtract it. Otherwise add it.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: M is not smaller than C, so add a thousand. C IS smaller than M, so subtract a hundred. Then M, add a thousand.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: X before C subtracts ten, C adds a hundred, I before V subtracts one, V adds five. Nineteen ninety-four, with a single rule.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One comparison replaces six special cases. Why does that work?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Because the notation is defined by that very property — a smaller symbol before a larger one is the only situation in which subtraction occurs. The six pairs are consequences of the rule, not the rule itself.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The last letter has nothing after it, so it is always added. That falls out naturally if you treat a missing successor as zero.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Enumerating the six subtractive pairs, which works but is longer and easier to get wrong. And forgetting that the final character has no successor and is therefore always added.

14.title: Longest Common Prefix
14.epTitle: What All the Charts Agree On

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Find the longest common prefix shared by an array of strings. Return an empty string if there is none.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Three charts of the same waters, drawn by three cartographers. How much of the beginning do all three agree on?

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Compare position zero across all three, then position one, and stop at the first disagreement?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is the vertical scan, and it is the best of the simple approaches — because it stops as soon as the answer is known, without examining the rest of any chart.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: All three start with f. All three have l next. Then 'o', 'o', 'i' — disagreement. Two characters.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And if one chart runs out before the others?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then the prefix cannot be longer than that chart, so the scan stops there too. The answer is bounded by the SHORTEST string, always.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: There's a horizontal version too — take the first chart as a running prefix and shrink it against each of the others.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Same complexity in the worst case, but it reads every chart even when the answer is empty. If the very first characters disagree, the vertical scan is finished after one comparison.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Indexing past the end of the shortest string. And returning the whole first string when the array has one element but forgetting the empty-array case, which must return "".

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of integers, find all unique triplets [a, b, c] such that a + b + c equals zero. Return the triplets in any order, with no duplicate triplets in the result.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: Yohoho — imagine the ship's ledger as a row of six entries, already sorted from biggest debt to biggest credit: minus four, minus one, minus one, zero, one, two. Somewhere in here are THREE entries that balance to exactly zero, with no entry counted twice.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Do we have to check every possible group of three? With six entries that's already twenty different trios!

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Not one at a time. The ledger is sorted, so we fix ONE entry as the anchor, then hunt the other two with a two-pointer sweep on the rest — the exact same trick as balancing a two-person split, just repeated for every possible anchor.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Anchor at minus four. Left pointer starts right after it, right pointer at the far end: minus one and two.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Minus four plus minus one plus two is minus three — too low. Only sliding the left pointer up can raise that sum, and it never catches up before the pointers cross. No triplet starts with minus four.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Anchor moves to the next entry: minus one. Left resets just after it, right resets to the far end.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Minus one plus minus one plus two is zero — balanced! Log this trio, then slide both pointers inward to keep hunting under the same anchor.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Left steps to zero, right steps to one: minus one plus zero plus one is zero again — a second balanced trio!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Next anchor candidate is another minus one — the same value we already anchored on. Skip it, or we'd just log the same two trios twice.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Anchor moves to zero: zero plus one plus two is three — too high, and the pointers are already meeting each other. Nothing there.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: Two trios, no repeats. The ledger balances to zero exactly twice. Yohoho!

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting to skip a repeated anchor value (or repeated left/right values right after logging a match) — without that skip, the same triplet gets logged multiple times whenever the sorted array has duplicate numbers.

17.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
17.epTitle: Every Name the Den Den Mushi Could Mean

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a string of digits from 2 to 9, return every letter combination the number could spell, using the standard telephone keypad mapping.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The transponder snail recorded a number, not a name. Each digit could be any of three letters, so we need every name it might have been.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Two digits, three letters each — nine names. Build them by choosing one letter for the first digit, then one for the second, and recording what you have when the digits run out.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So it's a tree. From the top, three branches for a, b and c. Under each of those, three more for d, e and f.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And the shape is always the same three lines. Choose a letter and append it. Recurse to the next digit. Then REMOVE the letter — un-choose — so the next branch starts from a clean path.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Why does removing matter? Can't I just build a new string each time?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: You can, and with strings it is often cleaner — a new string per branch has no shared state to corrupt. But with a shared list or array, the un-choose is what stops one branch's choices leaking into its sibling's.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And when we reach the bottom, we record the path. But if we record the list itself rather than a COPY, every result points at the same list — and by the end it's empty.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The single most common bug in this whole family. The path is one object, mutated all the way back up. Store a copy.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And an empty recording? No digits at all?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then the answer is an empty list, not a list containing the empty string. Guard it at the top — the recursion would otherwise record one meaningless result.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Appending the shared path object to the results instead of a copy, which yields a list of identical (usually empty) entries. And returning [""] rather than [] for empty input.

19.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
19.epTitle: Cutting the Rope N From the End

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the head of a linked list, remove the nth node from the end and return the head. Do it in one pass.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Cut the second rope from the end. But we can't see the end from here, and we're only allowed to walk the line once.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Count the length first, then walk again to the right spot? That's two passes.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Instead, hold the gap. Send one hand n steps ahead, then walk both hands together. When the leading hand reaches the end, the trailing hand is exactly n from it.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The gap does the counting for us. We never learn the length and never need to.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: To remove a node you need its PREDECESSOR, so stop the trailing hand one short — on the node before the one to cut.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And if the node to cut is the head itself? Then its predecessor doesn't exist.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is what the dummy head is for. Start both hands at a dummy in front of the list and the head suddenly has a predecessor like everything else. The special case disappears rather than being handled.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: One pass, constant space, and no branch for the head.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Whenever a list problem has an awkward case at the front, reach for a dummy before reaching for an if.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Stopping the trailing pointer on the node to delete rather than on its predecessor. And removing the head without a dummy, which needs a separate branch that is easy to get wrong.

20.title: Valid Parentheses
20.epTitle: The Seals of the Golden Bell

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a string of brackets — (), [] and {} — determine whether every bracket is closed by the correct type, in the correct order.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The bell tower's seals are nested inside one another, three different kinds. Every seal has to be closed by its own kind, and the innermost one has to close first.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So count them? Three round seals opened, three closed. Three square, three closed. Balanced.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Counting proves the numbers match, not that the nesting is right. Take an open round, an open square, a close round, a close square — perfectly balanced counts, and completely invalid.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Because you can't close the outer one while the inner one is still open. It's about ORDER, not quantity.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And 'the most recent thing that is still unresolved' is precisely what a stack holds. Push every opening seal. On a closing seal, the top of the stack must be its partner.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Round, square, curly go on. Then close curly — top is curly, they match, pop it. Close square — matches, pop. Close round — matches, pop. Empty at the end.

clips.speaker: robin

clips.line: Two and one, then four and three, and five sits alone so it stays put.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Count, reverse, stitch, advance. It's three easy problems stacked, and the stacking is the hard part.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a sorted array, remove duplicates in place so each value appears once, keeping the original order, and return the new length.

clips.line: The manifest is sorted, and Zeff only wants one barrel listed per kind. Same rule as before — in place, and whatever sits past the new length is irrelevant.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Sortedness is what makes this easy: identical values are guaranteed adjacent, so a barrel is a duplicate exactly when it matches the one just kept.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So the write pointer again — but the test is no longer against a fixed value, it's against whatever we most recently wrote.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Keep the first barrel unconditionally, then for each subsequent one ask whether it differs from the last keeper. If so, write it and advance.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And an empty manifest? There's no first barrel to keep.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So guard it, or start the write index at zero and let the loop handle everything — either is fine as long as you have decided which.

clips.line: Without sorting, this would need a set and O of n memory. The order in the input is doing real work.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is the recurring lesson of this whole island: read what the input guarantees, because the guarantee usually IS the algorithm.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Comparing against nums[read - 1] rather than against the last KEPT value. They coincide here, but the distinction matters the moment the rule changes to allow k copies.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Remove all occurrences of a value from an array in place, and return the number of elements that remain. The order of the kept elements may change, and what lies beyond the returned length does not matter.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The rotten barrels have to go over the side. We can't rent a second hold, and nobody cares what's left in the space after the good barrels.

clips.speaker: usopp

28.title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String

clips.line: Return the index of the first occurrence of needle in haystack, or -1 if it does not occur.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Find where a phrase first appears in the ship's log — the position, not merely whether it is there.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Try every starting position and compare forward from each. That's the obvious way.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And it is a perfectly good answer — n times m in the worst case, but far better in practice, because most comparisons fail on the first character.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: What makes the worst case bad?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Highly repetitive text — a log of a thousand a's searched for a thousand a's followed by a b. Every start matches almost to the end and then fails.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And the fix is to remember what we already matched, rather than throwing it away and restarting.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is KMP. Precompute, for each prefix of the phrase, the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix of it — then on a mismatch you know exactly how far you may skip without missing anything.

clips.speaker: nami

clips.speaker: robin

clips.speaker: _narrator

30.title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a string s and a list of words all of the same length, return every starting index in s where a substring is exactly a concatenation of all the words, each used once, in any order.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The vault passphrase is two words long — but the guard will accept them in EITHER order, and they must be spoken back to back with nothing in between. We have to find every place in this intercepted transmission where that happens.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Every arrangement of the words, searched for separately? With two words that's two arrangements. With ten words it's three and a half million.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: We never need the arrangements. All the words are the same length — three letters — so any valid stretch is just six letters split into two three-letter chunks. We only have to check that the multiset of chunks matches.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Read the transmission in three-letter chunks starting at position zero: 'bar', 'foo'. That is exactly our two words, each used once. Position zero is a hit.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: But chunks starting at position one would be 'arf', 'oot' — nonsense. So don't we have to restart the chunking at every single position?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Only three times, not eighteen. Every position falls into one of three alignments — offset zero, one, or two — and within one alignment the chunk boundaries never move. So run a sliding window three times, once per alignment.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Inside an alignment it is an ordinary window over chunks. Add a chunk on the right; if it isn't one of our words at all, throw the whole window away and start fresh after it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And if it IS one of our words but we've already used it as many times as the passphrase allows, we shrink from the left until that duplicate is legal again.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: When the window holds exactly as many chunks as there are words, and none is over its allowance, we record the start. Then slide one chunk on and keep going.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So the words list can repeat a word? 'foo' twice means we're allowed two 'foo' chunks and no more?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Exactly — which is why it is a count map rather than a set. A set would happily accept 'foo foo' when the passphrase was 'foo bar'. That single mistake is the difference between a working vault key and a locked door.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Using a set instead of a count map, which loses the requirement that a repeated word be present that many times. Also: on an unknown chunk, the window must be reset entirely rather than shrunk one chunk at a time.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: A once-sorted array has been rotated at an unknown pivot. Given the rotated array and a target value, find the target's index in O(log n) time, or return -1 if it isn't present.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The old dynasty stored these scrolls by year, earliest to latest. Then the tremor spun this shelf — it's no longer sorted start to end, but it's not random either. We want the scroll marked 20.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: So how do we search a sorted shelf that isn't sorted anymore?!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The FIRST scroll reads '50', bigger than the middle one — that proves the left side is the half that got wrapped around. The right side, 10 through 40, is still in honest year order, and 20 falls inside that range. So we hunt to the right.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Middle of what's left: scroll five, '30'. Our target is smaller, and this little stretch is still sorted — so 20 has to sit before it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which leaves exactly one scroll. Scroll four: '20'. Found.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: Three checks for seven scrolls! ...but how did you know WHICH half was the honest one?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: A single rotation only ever breaks the order in one place. So at every split, at least one half is still perfectly sorted — I just compare its two ends to know which one to trust, and rule out the other half entirely.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a sorted array, find the starting and ending index of a target value. Return [-1, -1] if it is absent. The whole thing must run in O(log n).

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The name appears more than once in the ledger, and we need both ends of the run — where it starts and where it stops.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Find it with a normal binary search, then walk outward until the name changes?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is fine until the whole ledger is that one name. Then walking outward reads every entry — linear, and precisely the case the problem is testing.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So instead of stopping when we find it, we keep searching. For the first end, keep going left even after a match.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Two boundary searches. The first index whose value is at least the target, and the first index whose value is greater than it. Those two bracket the run exactly.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: First index at least 8 is position three. First index greater than 8 is position five. So the run is three to four.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And absence falls out with no extra case. If the first boundary lands past the end, or the value there is not the target, the name is not in the ledger at all.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Two searches of log n each. Still logarithmic, whatever the run length.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And both are the same template with one character changed — less-than for the left edge, less-than-or-equal for the right. Learn one boundary search properly and you get this whole family for free.

clips.speaker: _narrator

35.title: Search Insert Position
35.epTitle: Where the New Name Goes on the Roster

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target, return the index of the target. If it is absent, return the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The Mink roster is kept in order. A new name arrives — where does it slot in? And if it's already there, where is it?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Both questions have the same answer: the first position whose name is not smaller than the newcomer. That single phrasing covers found and not-found alike.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So we're not really searching for the target — we're searching for a BOUNDARY. The point where 'smaller than the target' stops being true.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And that is what binary search actually needs. Not a sorted array as such, but a condition that is false, false, false, then true and stays true.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Determine whether a 9 x 9 Sudoku board is valid. Only the filled cells need checking: each row, each column and each of the nine 3 x 3 boxes must contain no repeated digit.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Dorry and Brogy have carved a duelling grid into the rock — nine by nine, split into nine blocks. A digit may not repeat in any row, any column, or any block.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Three separate checks, then? Scan all the rows, then all the columns, then all the blocks. Three passes over eighty-one cells.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Or one pass with three sets of records. Every cell belongs to exactly one row, one column and one block, so as you visit it you can file it in all three at once.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Row and column are easy — they're the coordinates. But which block is a cell in?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Integer division collapses a coordinate to its band: rows zero, one and two all divide to zero. Multiply the row band by three and add the column band, and the nine blocks number themselves in reading order.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So cell at row four, column seven: four over three is one, seven over three is two. One times three plus two is five. Block five.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then it is just three arrays of nine sets. Visit a filled cell, and if the digit is already recorded in any of its three sets, the grid is invalid. Otherwise record it in all three and move on.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Empty cells are simply skipped. We're asked whether the board is valid, not whether it can be finished.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: That distinction matters. A board can be perfectly valid and still have no solution at all. Nobody asked us to solve it.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Using modulo instead of division for the box index, which gives the offset within a band rather than the band itself. Also, checking solvability rather than validity — the problem only asks about the filled cells.

39.title: Combination Sum
39.epTitle: Exact Toll for Punk Hazard's Gate

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of distinct positive candidate numbers and a target, return every unique combination of candidates that sums exactly to the target. The SAME candidate may be reused any number of times, and combinations that use the same numbers in a different order do not count as different.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Punk Hazard's toll gate takes coins worth 2, 3, 6, or 7 — reuse any coin as many times as you like — and it must land on EXACTLY 7. Find every way to pay it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Brute-forcing every possible pile of coins gets messy fast. Better: keep adding coins and track the running total, but the moment it goes OVER 7, that pile is dead — stop right there.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And to avoid counting [2,3] and [3,2] as different piles, only add coins at the CURRENT position or later in the list — never go back to an earlier coin type.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Add a 2. Pile [2], sum 2.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Add another 2 (reuse allowed). Pile [2,2], sum 4.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Add a third 2. Pile [2,2,2], sum 6. Still under 7 — keep going.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: A fourth 2 would push the sum to 8 — over target. Dead end, undo it. Try 3 instead: pile [2,2,3], sum 7. EXACT MATCH — pay accepted!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Undo all the way back to empty. Try starting with 3 alone, or 6 alone — 3+3+3=9, 3+6=9, 6+6=12, 6+7=13 — every path through them overshoots 7 without ever landing on it exactly. All dead ends.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Last candidate: 7 alone. Pile [7], sum 7 — EXACT MATCH again!

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Two ways through the gate: three coins, or just the one big 7!

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Pruning the moment the sum passes 7 is what saves us — no point building a taller pile once it's already too heavy.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Copying the Subsets pattern exactly and recursing with i+1 instead of i. 42.title: Trapping Rain Water

clips.line: Given an elevation map where each bar has width 1, compute how much rain water it can trap.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Rain pools between the cliffs. How much does the whole coastline hold?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Think column by column rather than pool by pool. The water above any single column is decided by the tallest wall to its left and the tallest to its right — specifically, by the SMALLER of those two, minus the column's own height.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So precompute both, then one pass to add it up? That's three passes and two arrays, but it's easy to argue.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And there is a two-pointer version with no arrays at all. Walk inward from both ends, each side carrying the tallest wall it has seen.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The trick is knowing which side to move.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Always the SHORTER one. If the left maximum is below the right maximum, then for that column the smaller of the two IS the left maximum — whatever is still hidden on the right cannot lower it. So the column can be settled immediately.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: We don't need the true right maximum — only the knowledge that it's at least as tall as what we've already seen.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One pass, two numbers. That reasoning — 'I have enough information to commit, even without the full picture' — is what two-pointer arguments always come down to.

clips.speaker: _narrator

45.title: Jump Game II
45.epTitle: The Fewest Leaps Across the Stones

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Each position holds the maximum jump length from there. Starting at index 0, return the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index. Reaching it is guaranteed possible.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Stepping stones across the shallows. Each stone tells you the furthest you may leap from it — not the exact distance, the maximum. Fewest leaps to the far side.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Breadth-first search, treating each stone as a node? That would work, and it would give the shortest path.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: It would — and there is a way to do the same thing without a queue. Think in RINGS: everything reachable in one leap, then everything reachable in two.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So walk forward, tracking the furthest stone anything in the current ring can reach.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And when you arrive at the END of the current ring, you must leap — increment the count, and the new ring extends to the furthest point discovered so far.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: From stone zero the ring ends at index one. Standing there, we can reach index four — the far side. Two leaps.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: It's breadth-first search with the queue replaced by two integers. Same rings, no storage.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One detail: the loop must stop before the last stone. Arriving there is the goal, and counting a leap from it would add one too many.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Looping to the last index inclusive, which counts one jump too many on arrival. And greedily jumping to the furthest single stone each time, which is a different and incorrect rule.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of unique numbers, return every possible ordering (permutation) of them, in any order.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Three crewmates — 1, 2, 3 — need a lookout ORDER for the Crow's Nest. Unlike splitting loot, order matters here: [1,2,3] and [3,2,1] are different rotations.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Fill the rotation one slot at a time: pick any crewmate not already placed, add them to the line, and recurse. Once the line is full, record it — then undo the last pick and try the next unused crewmate in that slot.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Slot 1: place 1.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Slot 2: only 2 or 3 remain unused — place 2.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Slot 3: only 3 remains — place it. Line is full: [1,2,3] — rotation #1!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Undo slot 3, undo slot 2 — back to [1]. Now try 3 in slot 2 instead, since 2 was already tried there.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Slot 2: place 3. Slot 3: only 2 left — place it. [1,3,2] — rotation #2! Then fully undo back to an empty line.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Every branch under '1 first' is used up — two rotations found. Same process starting with 2 first, then with 3 first.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Starting with 2: [2,1,3] and [2,3,1]. Starting with 3: [3,1,2] and [3,2,1]. Same choose-recurse-undo dance, every time.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Six full rotations out of three lookouts!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: 3 choices for slot 1, times 2 for slot 2, times 1 for slot 3 — 3! = 6. Order matters, so it grows a lot faster than subsets did.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting to reset a crewmate's `used` flag (or fully undo the placement) after backtracking out of a branch. Leftover 'used' markers make later branches silently skip that crewmate, undercounting the permutations — the whole point of backtracking is that undoing a choice must restore the exact state from before it was made.

48.title: Rotate Image
48.epTitle: Turning the Map a Quarter Turn

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees clockwise, in place, without allocating another matrix.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The Log Pose reading means the chart has to be turned a quarter turn clockwise. And we only have the one sheet of paper — no copying it out.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Move each cell to where it ends up? Cell at row zero column zero goes to row zero column two, which pushes that one to row two column two...

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is the four-cycle version, and it is correct but fiddly — you rotate four cells at a time, layer by layer, and the loop bounds are easy to get wrong. There is a much easier route.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: First flip the chart about its main diagonal — swap the cell at row r column c with the one at row c column r. That turns every row into a column.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And then simply reverse each row left to right. Two easy operations instead of one hard one.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: How would I ever remember which order those go in?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Do not remember it — derive it. Write a two by two with four distinct values, do it both ways, and see which lands on the answer. It takes ten seconds and it settles the question permanently.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And if the Log Pose swings the other way — what turns the chart anti-clockwise?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Transpose, then reverse each COLUMN instead. Or equivalently, reverse the rows first and then transpose. Same two moves, different pairing.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One trap in the transpose itself: if I loop over every pair of coordinates, I swap each pair twice and end up exactly where I started.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So the inner loop starts at the outer index, touching only one side of the diagonal. That is the difference between a transpose and an expensive way of doing nothing.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Transposing with a full double loop, which swaps every pair twice and leaves the matrix unchanged — the inner loop must start at the outer index. And applying the two steps in the wrong order, which produces a counter-clockwise turn.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a list of strings, group together the strings that are anagrams of each other (same letters, different order). Return the groups in any order; the strings inside a group can be in any order too.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Six wanted-poster scrolls came off the same press, but the ink smudged and the letters got shuffled on half of them — eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat. Some of these are the SAME name in disguise!

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: How do we know which ones are really the same name spelled differently, without checking every scroll against every other scroll?

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: We don't compare scroll to scroll at all. Sort the letters INSIDE each name alphabetically first — two names that are anagrams of each other always collapse to the exact same sorted spelling. That sorted spelling becomes the label on a filing box.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: "eat" sorted is "a-e-t". No box with that label yet — open a new one.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: "tea" sorted is also "a-e-t" — straight into the same box as "eat".

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: "tan" sorted is "a-n-t" — a new label, a new box.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: "ate" sorted is "a-e-t" again — box one.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: "nat" sorted is "a-n-t" — box two.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: "bat" sorted is "a-b-t" — nothing matches. A third box.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Three boxes. One pass. Never opened a scroll twice.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Same crew, different aliases — can't fool a filing box! So, is any of these boxes food?

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Using a key that is not canonical (e.g. hashing the string as-is, or concatenating characters in input order) instead of a true signature — sorting the letters of each string (or building a 26-length character-count tuple) guarantees every anagram of a word produces the identical key.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Implement pow(x, n), raising x to the integer power n, where n may be negative.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Each blow doubles the force of the last. To reach the tenth blow, do we really have to throw all ten?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: No — square as you go. x squared is x times x. x to the fourth is that squared. x to the eighth is that squared again. Each step doubles the exponent rather than adding one to it.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So ten is eight plus two. Multiply the eighth-power blow by the second-power blow.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is exactly the binary form of the exponent. Every one-bit says 'include this squaring in the product'. Ten in binary is one-zero-one-zero, so the eighth and the second are taken.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Four multiplications instead of ten. And for a thousand, ten instead of a thousand.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Logarithmic in the exponent, because each round consumes one of its bits.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: What if the exponent is negative?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Invert the base and make the exponent positive. But in a fixed-width language, negating the most negative integer overflows — its positive counterpart does not exist. Convert to a wider type first, or handle that one value specially.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One value out of four billion, and it's the one they'll test.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Negating n when it is the most negative representable integer, which overflows. Also, repeated multiplication of floats accumulates rounding error — worth acknowledging, though the problem tolerates it.

52.title: N-Queens II
52.epTitle: The Sea Kings That Cannot See Each Other

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Return the number of distinct ways to place n queens on an n x n chessboard so that no two attack each other.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One Sea King per row of the trench, and no two may ever be in line of sight — not along a row, not down a column, not along either diagonal.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One per row is forced, so the recursion is by row: place a queen somewhere in row zero, then row one, and so on. Rows can never conflict, which removes a third of the checking immediately.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Columns are easy — a set of the columns already taken. But how do you check a diagonal quickly? Scanning the board every time would be slow.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Look at what stays constant along one. Going down-right, the row and column both increase, so their DIFFERENCE never changes. Going down-left, one rises as the other falls, so their SUM never changes.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So three sets — columns, differences, sums — and every safety check is three constant-time lookups.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then it is choose, recurse, un-choose over the columns of each row. Add to all three sets, descend, remove from all three.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And when a queen reaches the last row, that's one complete arrangement. We're only counting, so we don't even need to store the board.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Why does making the check fast matter so much? It's only three lookups either way.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Because a fast check is what lets you reject a placement immediately, and every rejection at row two removes an entire subtree of arrangements below it. In an exponential search, where you cut matters far more than how quickly you loop.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Scanning the board to test safety, which turns an O(1) check into O(n) and multiplies the whole exponential search. Also, both diagonal keys must be removed on the un-choose, not just the column.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of numbers, find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum, and return that sum. The subarray must contain at least one number.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: Zoro's fighting the whole Colosseum block in one go! Every round either builds him up or beats him down, and he can't skip a round in the middle — once he starts a run, he takes them in order.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: So the only choice I have is where to START and where to STOP. Which stretch of consecutive rounds leaves me strongest at the end?

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Just try every stretch! Start at round one, try all the endings, then start at round two... uh. That's every pair. With a hundred rounds that's thousands of runs.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: We don't need thousands. Walk forward once, and at every round ask exactly one question: is the run I'm carrying still helping me — or should I throw it away and start fresh right here?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Round one is minus two. There's no run behind me, so that IS the run. Carrying minus two — and it's the best we've seen, because it's all we've seen.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Round two is plus one. Now: minus two plus one is minus one — worse than just starting fresh at plus one. So we drop everything behind us. The run resets.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Round three, minus three. One minus three is minus two — but starting fresh here would be minus three, which is worse. So I keep dragging the run along. Being negative doesn't mean I abandon it; being a burden does.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Round four, plus four. Minus two plus four is two — but fresh is four. Fresh wins. Cut the run loose and start again at round four.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Minus one takes me to three. Plus two takes me to five. Plus one takes me to six. Every one of those is worth carrying — and six is the highest I've ever stood.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Rounds four through seven. Six. And you only walked the line once — no going back, no trying every pair.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Two numbers were enough the whole time: the run I'm in, and the best I've ever recorded. Notice they are separate — the run went negative twice, and the record never budged.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: So the rule is: if what you're carrying is dragging you down, drop it. But keep the memory of your best day! SHISHISHI!

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Initialising best = 0 quietly assumes an empty run is allowed. On an all-negative array it returns 0 instead of the largest single element. Seed both variables with nums[0] and scan from index 1.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an m x n matrix, return all its elements in spiral order — right along the top, down the right side, left along the bottom, up the left side, then inward.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Circling the sleeping dinosaur — all the way along one side, then turn, then along the next, tightening the loop each time round until there's nothing left in the middle.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So track four walls — top, bottom, left, right — and pull each one inward after you walk it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Walk the top row left to right, then lower the top wall. Walk the right column downward, then pull the right wall in. Walk the bottom row backwards, raise the bottom wall. Walk the left column upward, push the left wall in. Repeat.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Nine cells for a three by three. One two three, then six nine, then eight seven, then four, then five in the middle.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: But what about a matrix that's one row tall? You'd walk the top row, then try to walk the bottom row backwards — which is the same row again.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is the whole difficulty of this problem. After the top row and the right column are consumed, the walls may already have crossed. So before the bottom pass, re-check that top is still at or above bottom; before the left pass, that left is still at or before right.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Two extra checks, and only on the second two passes. The first two are always safe because the loop condition just proved it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Test it on a single row and a single column before you submit. Those two shapes catch this bug immediately, and a square matrix never will.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The alternative is counting: stop as soon as you've emitted as many cells as the matrix holds. Same effect, and some people find it easier to argue about.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Emitting the middle row or column twice on a matrix that is not square. The guard is a re-check of top <= bottom before the bottom pass and left <= right before the left pass — a 1 x 5 or 3 x 4 input exposes it instantly.

55.title: Jump Game
55.epTitle: The Stepping Stones to Fishman Island

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of non-negative integers where each element is the maximum jump length from that position, and starting at index 0, determine whether it's possible to reach the last index.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Five stepping stones across the current, each one lets you leap forward AT MOST as many stones as its power number says. Starting on stone 0, can the great Captain Usopp reach stone 4, the goal?

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: Just jump as far as you can, every time, right?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That instinct is almost right — let's make it precise. Walk the stones left to right and track the FARTHEST stone reachable so far. If we ever reach a stone that's beyond that farthest mark, we're stuck in the water. If the farthest mark ever reaches or passes the goal, we've made it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Stone 0, power 2: farthest reach becomes 0 + 2 = stone 2.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Stone 1 is within reach (1 ≤ 2). Its power 3 pushes us to 1 + 3 = stone 4 — already the goal stone!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Stone 2 is within reach (2 ≤ 4). Its power 1 only reaches stone 3 — no improvement, farthest stays 4.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Stone 3 is within reach (3 ≤ 4). Its power 1 only reaches stone 4 — still no improvement, farthest stays 4.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Stone 4, the goal itself, is within reach (4 ≤ 4). We're done — it's reachable!

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Fishman Island, here we come! And we didn't even need to know the EXACT path, just that we could always reach far enough!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: One pass, one running number. The second the current position outruns the farthest reach, stop — it's over.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Bailing out early the instant a stone with power 0 is seen, without first checking whether the farthest reach ALREADY carried you past that stone — a zero mid-array is only fatal if nothing earlier could jump over it.

56.title: Merge Intervals
56.epTitle: The Three Open Hours of Alubarna

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a list of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals and return the resulting set of non-overlapping intervals.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: We stole Baroque Works' patrol logs. Four watch shifts on the palace wall, sorted by the hour each one starts. We need to get Vivi's group in through a gap in the watch — not fight through it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: First shift: hours 2 to 5.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Next shift starts at hour 4 — before the first one even ends at 5. That's not a second watch, that's the SAME watch overlapping. Merge them: 2 to 8.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Hour 11 starts after hour 8 — nobody's watching in between. New block.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: But hour 12 overlaps THAT one before it's done at 13. Merge again: 11 to 16.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Two guarded stretches, start to finish: 2 to 8, and 11 to 16. Everything else — including the three hours between 8 and 11 — is open air.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: We didn't need to know who was on which shift, or when any ONE guard blinks. Just where the merged blocks end — and where they don't reach. That's our window.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Comparing the next interval's start against the PREVIOUS interval's original end instead of the merged block's (possibly extended) end — always extend with `max(current_end, next_end)`, never overwrite it, or a later, shorter interval can silently shrink an already-merged block.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: You are given a list of non-overlapping intervals, already sorted by start time, plus one new interval. Insert the new interval into the list, merging it with any existing intervals it overlaps, and return the resulting list of intervals — still sorted, still non-overlapping.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Two ships already have dock slots booked at Water 7: hours one to three, and hours six to nine. Now a third ship radios in wanting hours two to five — and it isn't on the schedule yet. Where does it fit?

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: If it doesn't overlap anybody, we just slot it in wherever it belongs by start hour and we're done. But if it DOES overlap an existing booking, we can't just staple it in — the two bookings have to become one longer one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So we walk the schedule once, in order, and ask three questions about each existing slot: does it end before the new one even starts? Does it start after the new one ends? Or does it overlap?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: First slot, one to three. It doesn't end before hour two — its end, three, is past our new booking's start. And it doesn't start after hour five either. That's overlap. We swallow it into the new booking: the low end stays one, the high end stretches to five.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Second slot, six to nine. Does it start after our now-grown booking ends at five? Yes — six is past five. No overlap. That means our merged booking is finished growing, and this slot stands entirely on its own, right after it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: One to five, then six to nine. Two slots on the board, in order — and the new ship folded straight into slot one without anybody reshuffling the whole schedule by hand.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: So the new ship didn't even need its OWN dock — it just moved into ship one's spot and made it bigger! SHISHISHI!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: One pass. Keep what ends before you start, merge whatever overlaps, keep what starts after you end.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting to append the growing new interval to the result if it never gets appended inside the loop — e.g. when the new interval overlaps nothing and belongs after every existing one, the sweep can finish without ever placing it. Always append the (possibly merged) new interval once, after the 'ends before' loop and before the 'starts after' loop, not conditionally inside either.

58.title: Length of Last Word
58.epTitle: The Last Word on the Signpost

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a string of words separated by spaces, return the length of the last word. There may be trailing spaces.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The signpost has been weathered and there are stray spaces trailing off the end. How long is the last actual word?

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Split on spaces and take the last piece? That works, but it builds a list of every word to look at one of them.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Walk backwards instead. Skip any trailing spaces, then count letters until you meet a space or run out of signpost.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Two loops, no allocation, and it stops as soon as it has the answer — even if the signpost is a thousand words long.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The trailing spaces are the whole trick, aren't they. Without skipping them first you'd count zero.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And a string that is entirely spaces has no last word at all — the answer is zero, and the second loop simply never runs.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Easy problems still have edge cases. This one has two, and both live at the end of the string.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is a good habit generally: when a problem mentions the end of something, check what happens when the end is ragged or empty.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting the trailing spaces, which gives a length of zero. And assuming there is always a last word — an all-space string must return 0.

61.title: Rotate List
61.epTitle: The Ring Road of Angel Island

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the head of a linked list, rotate it to the right by k places.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The ring road has to be shifted round by k — the last k stops come to the front, everything else slides back.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Move the last node to the front, k times? That's k walks of the whole road.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Do it in one move instead. Walk once to measure the length and reach the tail, then close the road into an actual ring by linking the tail back to the head.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And then just cut it open again in the right place.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The new head is k from the end, so it is length minus k from the front — and the cut goes immediately before it. One walk to find that point, one break, done.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And k can be enormous. Rotating a five-stop road by five hundred is the same as rotating it by zero.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So reduce k modulo the length first. If it comes out zero, the road is unchanged and you can return immediately — and if you have already closed the ring, you must be careful to reopen it.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Empty list, or a single stop — both are unchanged by any rotation.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Closing a list into a ring and cutting it elsewhere is a genuinely reusable move. Any 'shift everything round' problem is a ring waiting to be cut.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting k %= length, which makes a large k walk the list needlessly or overshoot. And leaving the ring closed when k reduces to 0, producing an infinite list.

63.title: Unique Paths II
63.epTitle: Counting the Roads Around the Rubble

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Count the distinct paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid, moving only right or down, where some cells are blocked by obstacles.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: How many different roads cross the ruins, right and down only — and some squares are buried under rubble and cannot be stepped on at all.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Counting rather than optimising, so the two predecessors are ADDED rather than compared. The ways to reach a square are the ways to reach the square above plus the ways to reach the square to its left.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And a blocked square? Do we skip it?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Set it to zero ways. Then it contributes nothing to anything downstream, automatically — no branching, no special case. Zero is the natural absorbing value for a counting DP.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So the obstacle removes every road through it just by being a zero. That's elegant.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The first row worries me. If one square in it is blocked, everything after it in that row is unreachable.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And the recurrence handles it correctly, provided the first row is built by propagation rather than being filled with ones. A blocked square makes it zero, and every square after it inherits that zero.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And if the start square itself is rubble, there are no roads at all.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which the same rule gives you for free: the start is set to zero, and everything downstream multiplies out to nothing. Encode the obstacle in the value and the special cases evaporate.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Filling the first row and column with ones before checking for obstacles — a blocked cell must zero everything after it in that row or column. Also, the start or end cell may itself be blocked.

64.title: Minimum Path Sum
64.epTitle: The Cheapest Road Across the Ruins

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an m x n grid of non-negative numbers, find a path from top-left to bottom-right that minimises the sum of the numbers along it. You may only move right or down.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Crossing the ruins costs something at every slab, and we may only step right or down. Find the cheapest crossing.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Because movement is one-way, any slab can only be reached from the slab above it or the slab to its left. So its cheapest arrival is its own cost plus the cheaper of those two.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And the first row can only be reached from the left, the first column only from above. Those are the base cases and they're just running totals.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Fill the rest row by row, and each slab needs only two already-finished neighbours. The bottom-right slab holds the answer.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The whole difference between this and the exponential version is that we ask about SLABS, not about paths. There are nine slabs and dozens of paths.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And each row only needs the row above it, so a single array of the width will do — reading its own previous value as 'left' and its unmodified value as 'up'.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: That's neat. The same slot holds 'up' before we write it and 'left' after.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is exactly why that loop must run left to right. Reverse it and 'left' has not been computed yet. The direction is load-bearing here, unlike in the triangle.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Getting the base cases wrong: the first row and first column have only one predecessor each, so they are running totals rather than a min of two. With the rolling array, the column loop must run left to right.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a large integer represented as an array of its digits, most significant first, increment it by one and return the resulting digits.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The tally of sake cups is written one digit per plank, and Kaido has called for one more. Add one to the tally.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Read the planks as a number, add one, write it back? That number can be hundreds of digits long — no integer type holds it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So work on the planks directly, from the right. If the last digit is below nine, add one to it and you are finished — no carry, nothing else to touch.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And if it's a nine, it becomes zero and the carry moves left.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Both planks are nines here, so both become zero and the carry runs off the front of the board entirely.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is the only case that changes the LENGTH of the tally. And it happens exactly when every digit was a nine — so the answer is a one followed by that many zeros.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So there's no need to track the carry through a loop at all. Walk backwards, and the first digit below nine ends it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Adding one is the simplest possible carry — it either stops at the first non-nine or it propagates all the way out. That is what makes this a two-line problem once you see it.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Converting the digits to an integer, which overflows for the large inputs this problem is built around. And forgetting the all-nines case, which is the only one that changes the array length.

67.title: Add Binary
67.epTitle: Two Tallies on the Same Scroll

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given two binary strings a and b, return their sum as a binary string.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Two tallies of Wano's rice stores, both kept in the old way — a stroke for each doubling. They have to be added, and the answer written in the same notation.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Convert both to ordinary numbers, add them, convert back! ...Except these scrolls run to thousands of strokes, and no ordinary number holds that.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So add them the way you were taught to add on paper: right to left, column by column, carrying what spills over. The only difference is that a column spills at two rather than at ten.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Rightmost column: zero and one. That's one, no carry. Next: one and one. That's two — write zero, carry one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Next column: zero and zero, plus the carry of one. That is one, carry nothing. Then one and one, which is two again — write zero, carry one.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: And now both scrolls are exhausted but the carry is still standing. It gets its own column at the front.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is the whole trap in this problem. The loop must keep going while EITHER string has digits left OR a carry is outstanding — three conditions, not two.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And the two scrolls needn't be the same length. Padding them first would work, but treating a missing digit as zero is simpler and costs nothing.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One more thing worth knowing. Each column here is a single-bit adder: the digit written is the exclusive-or of the three inputs, and the carry is set when at least two of them are one. That is literally how the hardware does it.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Ending the loop when both strings run out, dropping a final carry — the input "1" + "1" then returns "0" instead of "10". Also remember the result is built backwards and must be reversed.

68.title: Text Justification
68.epTitle: The Last Page of the Log

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Format an array of words into lines of exactly maxWidth characters, fully justified. Extra spaces go to the leftmost gaps first. The final line is left-justified.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The log has to be set in justified columns — every line exactly the same width, spaces spread between the words, and the final line left-aligned like a signature.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Nothing here is clever, is it. It's just a lot of rules, all of which have to be right at once.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is exactly what this problem tests. Do it in two clearly separated jobs: first decide WHICH words go on the line, then decide HOW to space them.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Packing is greedy — keep adding words while they fit, remembering that each new word needs at least one space before it.

clips.speaker: robin
