clips.line: Then the spacing. Take the leftover width, divide it among the gaps, and give the remainder one extra space each to the LEFTMOST gaps. That is what 'extra spaces on the left' means, precisely.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And a line holding just one word has no gaps at all, so dividing would be dividing by zero.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So a single-word line is left-justified and padded on the right — the same treatment as the final line. Two special cases that resolve to the same rule.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The way to survive this is to write the two jobs as separate functions and test them apart.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And to read the specification twice before writing anything. Almost every failure on this problem is a misread rule rather than a broken algorithm.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Dividing by the gap count on a single-word line, which is zero. And justifying the last line, which must be left-aligned with a single space between words and padding on the right.

69.title: Sqrt(x)
69.epTitle: Guessing the Height of the Skull Dome

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a non-negative integer x, return the square root of x rounded down to the nearest integer, without using any built-in exponent function.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The Skull Dome's height squared is written on the gate, and we need the height itself — rounded down, and without any convenient root button.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Squaring is monotone: bigger guesses give bigger squares, always. So 'is this guess squared at most x' is false-then-true reversed — true, true, true, then false. That is a boundary, and boundaries are binary searched.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So guess the middle, square it, and throw away half the range depending on whether it overshoots.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: We want the LARGEST guess whose square does not exceed x. So when a guess fits, keep it as the best so far and search higher; when it overshoots, search lower.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: For eight: guess four, sixteen is too big. Guess two, four fits — remember it. Guess three, nine is too big. Answer two.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One trap in fixed-width languages: squaring a guess near the top of the range overflows. Compare with division instead — is the guess at most x divided by the guess — and nothing ever grows.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And zero and one? The range has to include them, and the loop mustn't divide by zero.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Start the search at one and answer zero separately, or start at zero and guard the division. Either is fine, so long as you have decided which — that is the sort of thing worth saying out loud rather than discovering in a failing test.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Computing mid * mid, which can overflow near the top of the range in a fixed-width language — compare mid <= x // mid instead. And remembering that the answer is rounded down, so 8 gives 2, not 3.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: You're climbing a staircase with n steps. On each move you can climb either 1 step or 2 steps. Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Five steps up to the crow's nest! On every move I can hop up 1 step or 2 steps. How many different ways could I hop all the way to the top?

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: If we try to list every possible sequence of hops by hand it balloons fast. Better to build the answer step by step, using the answers for SMALLER staircases we've already solved.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Base cases first. Standing at step 0 already, doing nothing, counts as exactly 1 way. And there's exactly 1 way to reach step 1 — a single hop.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Every step after that: you either hopped 1 from the step before it, or hopped 2 from the step before THAT. So ways(step) = ways(step-1) + ways(step-2).

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Step 2: ways(1) + ways(0) = 1 + 1 = 2.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Step 3: ways(2) + ways(1) = 2 + 1 = 3.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Step 4: ways(3) + ways(2) = 3 + 2 = 5.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Step 5, the crow's nest itself: ways(4) + ways(3) = 5 + 3 = 8.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Eight different ways up, and we barely climbed at all — we just added two numbers, five times!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: You never need the whole staircase in memory, either. Just the last two numbers.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Solving this with naive top-down recursion and no memoization — the same sub-staircases (like ways(2)) get recomputed exponentially many times, blowing up to O(2^n) instead of O(n).

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an absolute Unix-style path, return its simplified canonical form: a single leading slash, no trailing slash, no "." or ".." segments, and no repeated slashes.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Cricket's map of Jaya is written as a trail, but it doubles back on itself. Some steps say 'stay put' and some say 'go back one'. We need the trail it actually describes.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Cut the trail at every slash and treat each piece as a token. Then the meaning of each token is simple: a real name moves you forward, '..' moves you back, and '.' or an empty piece does nothing.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Go back one — that's undoing the most recent step. Which is a stack again.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Push 'a'. Then a dot, which is ignored. Push 'b'. Then '..', which pops 'b'. Then another '..', which pops 'a'.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And now the stack is empty and there's ANOTHER '..'. Do we go back past the beginning?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is nowhere to go. The root is its own parent, so a pop on an empty stack is simply ignored. That guard is the single most missed line in this problem.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Then push 'c'. And the answer is a slash joined between everything left on the stack, with a slash at the front.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Splitting on the slash handles the repeated and trailing slashes for free — they simply produce empty tokens, which we already ignore. No separate cleaning pass needed.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And if everything pops away, the answer is just a single slash — not an empty string.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Popping an empty stack on "/..", which either crashes or produces nonsense — the root is its own parent. Also, a name like "..." is an ordinary directory, not a special token.

72.title: Edit Distance
72.epTitle: The Fewest Corrections to the Poneglyph

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given two words, return the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions or replacements needed to turn the first into the second.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The copied poneglyph differs from the original. We need the smallest number of corrections — inserting a glyph, deleting one, or replacing one — to make them agree.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Three possible moves at every point. Trying all sequences of them is hopeless.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So ask a smaller question: the cost of turning the first i glyphs into the first j glyphs. That is a table, and every cell has exactly four ways to be reached.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: If the two glyphs match, nothing needs doing — the cost is whatever it took to fix everything before them. The diagonal, for free.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And if they differ, take the cheapest of three neighbours and add one: the cell above is a deletion, the cell to the left is an insertion, the diagonal is a replacement.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Each neighbouring cell is one edit away from this one. That's a very clean way to remember which is which.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The base cases are the costs of building from nothing: turning an empty word into j glyphs costs j insertions, and turning i glyphs into nothing costs i deletions. Those are the first row and column.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And each row only needs the one above it, so two arrays are enough if we only want the number.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: If they want the actual list of corrections, keep the full table and walk back through it from the corner. That is the usual price of asking for the solution rather than its cost.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Base cases that are not the empty-prefix costs — dp[i][0] must be i and dp[0][j] must be j, not zero. And forgetting that a match costs nothing rather than costing one.

73.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
73.epTitle: The Rows and Columns That Burned

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an m x n matrix, if an element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0. Do it in place, ideally with O(1) extra space.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Wherever a fire has started on the map, the whole row and the whole column burn. Mark them all — but we can't afford a second map to work on.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Easy — walk the map, and whenever I find a fire, zero out its row and column right away.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And then you meet one of the zeroes you just wrote, and treat it as a new fire. The burning spreads until the entire map is black. Zeroing as you go is the trap here.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So record first, act second. Two sets — which rows burn, which columns burn — then a second pass to apply them.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is correct and costs O(m + n) space, which is a perfectly good answer. But the follow-up asks for constant, and the map can hold its own notes: use the first row and first column as the marker strips.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So a fire at row three column five writes a zero into row zero column five, and row three column zero. The marks live inside the map.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: With one complication: the first row and first column are both markers AND data. So before anything else, record separately whether each of them originally contained a zero.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Then apply the marks to the interior, and only at the very end use the two saved flags to burn the first row and first column themselves.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Order matters twice over — record before acting, and do the marker strips last so we don't destroy the notes while reading them.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Zeroing rows and columns during the first pass, which makes written zeroes indistinguishable from original ones and blackens the whole matrix. And forgetting the two flags for the marker strips, so the first row and column are wrong.

74.title: Search a 2D Matrix
74.epTitle: The Chart That Reads as One Long Line

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Search a target in an m x n matrix where each row is sorted and the first value of each row is greater than the last value of the previous row.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The Zou chart is drawn in bands. Each band runs in order, and every band starts after the previous one ends. Is depth 3 marked anywhere on it?

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Binary search each band in turn? That's m searches of log n each.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Read the guarantee again. Every band starts after the previous one ends — so if you laid all the bands end to end, the whole chart is ONE sorted line. There is nothing two-dimensional about it except the drawing.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So binary search over positions zero to m times n minus one, and convert a position back to a band and an offset when I need to read it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Division gives the band, modulo gives the offset within it — the same pairing as the Sudoku box index, used the other way round.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Twelve cells, so the middle is position five: band one, offset one — that's 11. Too big, so look left. Then position two: band zero, offset two — that's 5. Still too big. Then position one: 3. Found.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One search instead of three. Log of twelve rather than three lots of log four.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is a sister problem that looks almost identical — rows and columns each sorted, but the bands do NOT chain. That one is not a sorted line, and this trick fails on it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: For that one you walk from the top-right corner: too big means go left, too small means go down. O of m plus n. Different guarantee, different tool.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Applying this to LeetCode 240, where rows and columns are sorted but the rows do not chain — the flattened array is not sorted there and the search silently returns wrong answers.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a string s and a string t, find the smallest contiguous window (substring) of s that contains every character of t, including matching counts for repeated characters. Return that substring, or an empty string if no such window exists.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: This parchment reads A-D-O-B-E-C-O-D-E-B-A-N-C, and somewhere inside it is the SMALLEST possible stretch that still holds one A, one B, and one C. Find it, and only it gets copied out!

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: Just find any place where A, B, and C are all sitting close together, right? Why does it matter if it's the SMALLEST one?

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Because every letter of parchment we copy costs us ink and time — the smaller the excerpt, the less we haul back to the ship.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So: grow a window from the right until it holds every letter we need, then shrink it from the left as far as it'll still hold all of them, recording the smallest valid window each time. Expand to satisfy, shrink to tighten.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Expanding right — A, D, O, B, E, C. The moment C lands, at index five, I finally have one A, one B, one C. First valid window: index zero through five.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Try shrinking from the left — but dropping index zero throws away my only A. Invalid. So I stop shrinking there and keep pushing the right edge instead.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: O, D, E, B go by — nothing new needed — until index ten brings a second A. Valid again, but now the window stretches all the way from index one to index ten.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Now shrink hard — D, O, that extra B, and E all peel off the left edge without losing A, B, or C, since I still have the C at index five and the new A at index ten.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One more drop takes the C at index five with it — invalid. Stop shrinking, push right again.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: N goes by, then a second C lands at index twelve. Valid once more, window six through twelve.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Shrink again — O, D, E, and that extra B all peel off, and I still hold my A, my B, my C. Index nine through twelve: B, A, N, C. Four letters — the smallest yet.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Try to drop the B at index nine and the window loses its only B — invalid, and there's no more parchment to the right. Four letters is as small as it gets.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! BANC! ...is that a snack?

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Checking window validity as "does every needed character appear at least once" instead of "does every needed character appear at least as many times as in t" — this breaks the moment t has a repeated character (e.g. t = "AAB"), since a window holding only one A would incorrectly count as valid.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given two integers n and k, return all possible combinations of k numbers chosen from the range 1 to n.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Four candidates for the landing party, and we can take two. Every possible pair, listed once — and one-and-two is the same party as two-and-one.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So order doesn't matter. How do I stop myself listing the same party twice in a different order?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Fix an order and never go backwards. Each level of the recursion is handed a starting point, and it may only choose from there onward. That single index makes duplicates impossible.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Pick one, then the next level starts at two. Pick two, party complete: one and two. Un-choose, pick three: one and three. Then one and four.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then back up, start from two, and you get two-three and two-four. Then three-four. Six parties, none repeated — and we never even considered two-one.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: There's a smarter cut here, isn't there? Once I'm at candidate four with nobody chosen yet, there aren't enough people left to fill the party.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Exactly. If the numbers remaining are fewer than the slots still to fill, that whole branch is dead. Bound the loop so it never starts a party it cannot finish.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Which for large n and small k throws away a huge amount of pointless walking.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And this is the difference between combinations and permutations, in one variable. A start index means order does not matter; a used-set means it does. Choose the wrong one and you are solving the wrong problem.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Looping from 1 every level, which produces permutations and duplicates. And skipping the pruning bound, which explores branches that provably cannot reach k elements.

79.title: Word Search
79.epTitle: The Name Carved Through the Coral

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an m x n grid of letters and a word, return true if the word can be spelled by walking through adjacent cells (up, down, left, right) without reusing a cell.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The name is carved through the coral, letter by letter, turning corners — but never crossing itself. Is 'ABCCED' really in there?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Try every cell as a possible first letter. From a matching cell, walk to each of the four neighbours looking for the next letter, and so on.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And 'never crossing itself' means marking cells as used. But used only along the CURRENT path — a cell blocked by one attempt has to be free for the next.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So the mark goes on when you step in, and comes off when you step out — success or failure. Choose, recurse, un-choose, exactly as always.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: A at the top-left. B to its right. C next. Then C below. Then E, then D. All six letters, none reused.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The cheapest saving is to check the letter BEFORE recursing, not after arriving. Rejecting a neighbour without a function call removes four branches at every level.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Is there a way to bail out early on a hopeless word?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Count the letters on the board first. If the word needs three 'Z's and the board holds two, you can answer before searching at all. And if the word's last letter is rarer than its first, search it backwards.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Both of those are cheap checks that can save an enormous search. I like that they cost almost nothing to add.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Clearing the visited mark only on success, which blocks cells for every later path. And forgetting that the same letter may be reachable from several directions, so an early match does not mean the rest of the word follows.

80.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
80.epTitle: Two Barrels of Each, No More

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a sorted array, remove duplicates in place so each value appears at most twice, and return the new length.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: New rule from the quartermaster: two of each kind may stay, a third is over the side.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Count how many of each we've kept as we go? That means an extra variable and a reset whenever the value changes.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is something neater. A barrel would be a THIRD copy exactly when it equals the keeper two positions back. So compare against the keeper at write minus two — and no counter is needed at all.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Because if it matches two keepers back, and the manifest is sorted, everything between them is that same value too.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The first two barrels are always kept unconditionally, so the write index starts at two and the comparison is always in range.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And it generalises. Allow k copies and you compare against write minus k.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is the reason to phrase the comparison against the keepers rather than the reads. Write it that way for the simple version and the harder one is a single character.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One character. I'd have written a counter and a reset and probably got the reset wrong.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Comparing against read positions rather than write positions, which breaks once the write pointer lags. And forgetting that the first k elements are kept unconditionally so the index stays in range.

82.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II
82.epTitle: Every Trace of the Repeated Name

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the head of a sorted linked list, delete every node that has a duplicate, leaving only the values that appear exactly once.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The roster has duplicate names, and the rule is harsh: if a name appears twice, EVERY copy of it is struck out. Not one kept — none.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: That's different from the usual de-duplication, where you keep one of each.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is why the pointer you carry is different too. Here you must stand on the node BEFORE a run, because if the run turns out to be a duplicate you have to skip the whole thing.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So look ahead: if the next node and the one after it share a value, walk forward past every node with that value, then link across the entire run.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And crucially, do NOT advance the predecessor in that case — the node now sitting after it has not been examined yet and might begin another run.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Two runs back to back. If you advanced blindly after skipping the threes, the fours would slip through.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The head itself may be part of a run, so a dummy in front is required rather than merely convenient.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Sorted input is doing the heavy lifting, isn't it. Duplicates are guaranteed adjacent, so a run is a local thing.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Unsorted, you would need a counting pass first. The sortedness is what makes one walk enough.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Advancing the predecessor after skipping a run, which misses a run that starts immediately afterwards. And keeping one copy of a duplicated value — that is the easier sibling problem (LeetCode 83), not this one.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a linked list and a value x, reorder it so that all nodes less than x come before all nodes greater than or equal to x, preserving the original relative order within each group.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Light clouds to the front, heavy clouds to the back — but within each group, the order they were in must be kept exactly.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Swap nodes around in place until they're sorted?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Far easier: build two separate chains. Walk once, and append each cloud to the light chain or the heavy chain. Then join the two.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: One and two go left. Four, three and five go right. Then link the light tail to the heavy head.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Appending in the order encountered preserves the relative order within each group for free — that is what makes this stable without any extra effort.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Two dummy heads, one per chain, so neither needs a first-node special case.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And one line that must not be forgotten: terminate the heavy chain. Its last node still points wherever it did in the original list, which can easily be back into the light chain.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: A cycle, in other words. The output looks right until something tries to walk to the end of it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Splitting into buckets and concatenating is a pattern well beyond lists — it is how radix sort works, and how stable partitions are done generally.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting high_tail.next = None, which leaves the original forward pointer intact and usually creates a cycle. Also, swapping node values instead of re-linking is fragile and loses the point of the exercise.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Merge two sorted arrays into the first one, which has exactly enough spare room at its end. Do it in place.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Two crew rosters, both already in order. The first has empty berths at the end — exactly enough for the second. Merge them without renting a second ship.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Start at the front and insert each name where it belongs? Every insert shoves everyone after it one berth along.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So fill from the BACK instead. The free berths are at the end, so start there and write the LARGEST remaining name each time.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And the crucial property: the write position is always at or behind both read positions, so a write can never land on a name you have not read yet.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Six against three — six is larger, so it goes in the last berth. Then five. Then three from the first roster. Then two, two, one.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And what happens when one of the two rosters runs out before the other?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: If the FIRST runs out, whatever remains of the second still has to be copied in. If the second runs out, the rest of the first is already sitting in exactly the right place — nothing to do.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: That asymmetry is the one thing worth remembering here. Everything else falls out of writing backwards.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Merging from the front, which overwrites unread values. And forgetting that leftovers in nums2 must still be copied when nums1 is exhausted, while leftovers in nums1 are already in place.

92.title: Reverse Linked List II
92.epTitle: The Detour That Only Touched the Middle

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the head of a singly linked list and two 1-indexed positions left and right (left <= right), reverse only the nodes from position left to position right, leaving the rest of the list untouched, and do it in a single pass without extra data structures.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Same trail, five signs this time: one through five. But the merchant only wants the MIDDLE stretch flipped — signs two through four. Signs one and five stay exactly as they are.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And we still only get one walk down the trail — no rebuilding it from scratch, no spare pile of signs on the side.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: First, walk to the sign just before position two — that's sign one. Call it the anchor. Everything after the anchor is the stretch we're allowed to touch.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Curr starts at sign two — it will end up as the TAIL of the flipped stretch, so it stays put the whole time. Each round, I grab whatever sign currently sits right after curr, and re-hang it directly after the anchor instead.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Round one: the sign right after curr is three. Pull it out, hang it right after the anchor. Trail now reads one, three, two, four, five.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Round two: curr — still sign two — now has sign four sitting right after it. Pull four out, hang it right after the anchor too. Trail reads one, four, three, two, five.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That's right minus left — two rounds — and positions two through four are fully flipped. I never touched sign one or sign five.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So sign one and sign five never even noticed anything happened?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Exactly. That's the whole point of stopping the anchor exactly one sign before the range — everything outside it just stays wired to whatever the range's new ends turn out to be.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI, half a trail flipped and nobody had to redraw the whole map!

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Skipping the dummy node when left = 1 — with no real predecessor to serve as the anchor, the very first reassignment has nothing to attach to and crashes or silently drops the new head.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given strings s1, s2 and s3, determine whether s3 is formed by interleaving s1 and s2, preserving the internal order of each.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Two voices came through on the same channel, cut together. Each voice's own words are in order, but they alternate unpredictably. Is this recording really those two?

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Greedily take whichever voice matches the next sound? If both match, take the first?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is the trap. When both voices could supply the next sound, the choice matters — one leads to a valid parse and the other to a dead end, and you cannot tell which without looking ahead.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So we'd have to try both and backtrack. Exponential.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Unless we notice that the state is small. All that matters is how many sounds we have taken from each voice — i from the first and j from the second. And i plus j is always our position in the recording.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So there are only m times n states, not two-to-the-length paths. And each one asks a simple question: can I get here by taking one more from the first voice, or one more from the second?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Two dimensions, because two things move independently. That is what tells you this is a 2-D table rather than a 1-D one.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And there's a free rejection before any of it: if the lengths don't add up, it can't possibly be an interleaving.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Each row needs only the row before it, so the table collapses to a single array of the second string's length. The two-dimensional thinking stays; the storage does not have to.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Greedily consuming whichever string matches, which fails whenever both match and only one choice leads to a solution. Also, the length check len(s1) + len(s2) == len(s3) is a necessary precondition.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is a valid binary search tree (BST): for every node, ALL values in its left subtree must be smaller than the node's value, and ALL values in its right subtree must be larger — not just the node's immediate children, but every descendant at every depth.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Sengoku found this filed as a proper Bounty Ledger — a search tree, sorted so anyone can find a name by going left for smaller, right for bigger! But is it REAL, or forged?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The rule for a real one is strict: at EVERY node, everything in its left branch must be smaller, and everything in its right branch must be bigger — no matter how many levels down.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Can't we just check each entry against its own parent? That seems like less work.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That's the trap. A node has to obey EVERY ancestor above it, not just the one directly above. So as I go down, I'll carry a valid range — a floor and a ceiling — that narrows at each branch.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Root: 10, range is wide open. Fine. Its left branch must now stay below 10; its right branch must stay above 10.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Left to 5, range (-inf, 10): 5 fits, no children to check. That whole branch is clean.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Right to 15, range (10, inf): 15 fits. Its left child now inherits BOTH bounds — must stay above 10 (from the root) AND below 15 (from its own parent).

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: 15's left child is 6. Range required: (10, 15). 6 is below 15, sure — but it is NOT above 10. Forged.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And there's the con — if we'd only compared 6 to its direct parent, 15, it would've looked perfectly fine. The root's rule has to follow every entry all the way down.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! One sneaky little 6 stuffed two levels deep, and the WHOLE ledger's a fake!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Answer: false. We didn't even need to check 20 once the left side broke it.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Comparing each node only to its immediate parent instead of tracking the full inherited (low, high) range from every ancestor. That naive check would wrongly accept [10,5,15,null,null,6,20] as valid, since 6 < 15 looks fine locally even though 6 violates the root's rule.

100.title: Same Tree
100.epTitle: Two Blueprints, Compared Rivet by Rivet

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the roots of two binary trees, determine whether they are identical — the same structure and the same values at every node.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Two blueprints for the same ship. Iceberg wants to know whether they are truly identical — same shape, same numbers, no differences anywhere.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Recursion on trees is one honest question: what do I need from my children, and what do I hand my parent? Here the answer is a yes or a no, and it is the AND of both children's answers.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So at each pair of nodes: are they both absent? Then they match. Is exactly one absent? Then they differ. Otherwise compare the values and recurse on both sides.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The two-nodes-absent case is what makes it terminate. And 'exactly one absent' is the structural difference — the second blueprint has its 2 on the other side.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is why comparing the traversals alone is not enough. Two different trees can share a preorder sequence unless the nulls are recorded too.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So the shape has to be compared directly, node against node — not flattened first.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And the comparison short-circuits: the moment one side disagrees, the whole thing is false and nothing further needs visiting.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Three lines, once you have the three cases straight. The cases are the work.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Comparing flattened traversals without recording nulls — [1,2] and [1,null,2] both preorder to "1 2". And handling only one of the two null cases, which crashes on the other.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is a mirror image of itself about its centre.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The shipyard is supposed to be perfectly symmetric — everything on the left mirrored on the right, all the way down.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So compare the left subtree with the right subtree. But not node for node in the same direction — mirrored.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which means the recursion carries TWO pointers that move in opposite directions. The left one's left child pairs with the right one's RIGHT child, and vice versa.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: That crossing is the entire problem, isn't it. Compare them in the same direction and you'd be checking whether the two halves are identical, not mirrored.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Exactly. Two nodes mirror when their values agree AND the outer pair mirrors AND the inner pair mirrors.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And both absent is a match, exactly one absent is a mismatch — the same two null cases as comparing two trees.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The iterative form pushes nodes onto a queue IN PAIRS, which keeps the mirroring explicit rather than relying on the recursion to carry it.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Checking a whole level for being a palindrome would also work, but you'd have to include the nulls or the shape slips through.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Comparing left.left with right.left, which tests whether the halves are identical rather than mirrored. And forgetting that a level check must include nulls, or [1,2,2,null,3,null,3] passes.

102.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
102.epTitle: Clearing the Watchtower, Floor by Floor

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the root of a binary tree, return the values of its nodes grouped level by level, from top to bottom, and left to right within each level.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The Marine watchtower has three floors of guards: the commander alone at the top — room three. Below, two lieutenants — rooms nine and twenty. Below THEM, two grunts — rooms fifteen and seven, both guarding under room twenty.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: We are not sneaking straight down to the grunts. We clear a floor COMPLETELY before descending to the next one — record every room on this floor, then move to their doors.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That's a queue, not a stack. Push the root in first: room three. Queue: [3].

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Before draining, I snapshot how many rooms are on this floor — right now, just one. Pop room three, record it as this level's list, and push its two children, nine and twenty, onto the back of the queue.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: New floor, new snapshot: two rooms waiting. Pop room nine — it has no children, nothing to push. Pop room twenty — push ITS two children, fifteen and seven, onto the back.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Final floor: two rooms, fifteen and seven. Pop both, neither has children, nothing more gets pushed. Queue is empty — we've cleared every floor.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So the snapshot number is what keeps us from mixing a grunt from THIS floor in with a lieutenant from the last one?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Exactly — grab that count once, drain exactly that many before you check the count again. New children pushed mid-floor never get counted until the NEXT floor's snapshot.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Top floor first, then both floors under it, together, never skipping ahead! Now let's go get the commander!

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Checking the queue length WHILE draining the current level instead of snapshotting it once beforehand — children you just pushed get counted as part of the current level and everything smears into one long list.

103.title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Return the level-order traversal of a binary tree in zigzag order: the first level left to right, the next right to left, and so on.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The signal relay only works if each floor is read in the opposite direction to the floor above. Top floor left to right, next floor right to left, and back again all the way down.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Easy — I'll flip which child I put in the queue first on alternate floors. Left first, then right first, then left first...

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is the trap, and it is a subtle one. Changing the enqueue order does not only reverse the next floor — it scrambles the floor after that, because those children are enqueued from a parent order you have already disturbed.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So keep the walk completely boring. Always left child then right child, every single level, no exceptions.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And handle the zigzag where it belongs — at presentation. Build each level in the natural order, then reverse it if the level index is odd.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Level zero: just three. Even level, leave it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Level one collects nine then twenty. Odd level — reverse it. Twenty, nine.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Level two collects fifteen then seven. Even level — leave it alone.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: If reversing a list per level offends you, collect into a double-ended structure and push to the front on odd levels instead. Same result, no reversal pass — but the reversal is O(width) and the traversal is already O(n), so it changes nothing asymptotically.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Keep the machinery dumb, put the cleverness in the output. I like that better than trying to be clever inside the queue.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Alternating which child is enqueued first. It appears to work on level two and then quietly produces the wrong order on level three and below, because the parents were already out of order when their children were queued.

104.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
104.epTitle: How Deep Do the Tunnels Go?

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth — the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to the farthest leaf node.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: This ruin has branching tunnels — from the entrance, LEFT goes to a passage, RIGHT goes to another. I want to know how many tunnel-lengths deep the FARTHEST dead end goes.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Ask each branch how deep IT goes, and trust the answer. A tunnel with no branches past it is one level deep, all by itself.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Left branch from the entrance, room nine: no further branches. Depth one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Right branch from the entrance, room twenty: not a dead end — it splits again into room fifteen and room seven. Ask THEM first.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Room fifteen: no further branches. Depth one. Room seven: same, no further branches. Depth one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So room twenty's depth is one MORE than the deeper of its two children — both are depth one, so room twenty is depth two.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Back at the entrance: left branch was depth one, right branch was depth two. The entrance's own depth is one more than the DEEPER of the two — one more than two.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Three tunnel-lengths deep, straight down through room twenty and room fifteen or room seven! Let's go find treasure!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Every dead end reports back up. No need to check the whole map at once.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Returning 0 for a leaf node instead of 1 (or forgetting the +1 for the current node) — an easy off-by-one that undercounts the depth of every path by exactly one level.

105.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
105.epTitle: Rebuilding the Ship From Two Manifests

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the preorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree with distinct values, reconstruct the tree.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The ship's frame was catalogued twice, in two different orders, and the drawing itself is lost. Can we rebuild it from the two lists alone?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Each list gives one thing the other cannot. Preorder visits the root FIRST, so its first entry names the root immediately.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And inorder visits everything on the left, then the root, then everything on the right. So finding the root inside the inorder list splits it into the two subtrees.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Root is 3. In the inorder list, 9 lies to its left and 15, 20, 7 to its right — so the left subtree holds one node and the right holds three.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And those sizes tell us how to cut the preorder list too. The next one entry is the whole left subtree; the three after that are the right.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then recurse on each half with the same rule. Every node is created exactly once.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The 'find the root in the inorder list' step worries me. If that's a linear scan every time, it's quadratic.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So index the inorder positions in a map once, up front. Then the split is a lookup and the whole build is linear. And note that distinct values are a precondition — with duplicates, the split is ambiguous.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Searching the inorder list linearly at every level, which is quadratic on a degenerate tree. And assuming duplicates are fine — they make the split ambiguous and the problem unsolvable.

106.title: Construct Binary Tree from Inorder and Postorder Traversal

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the inorder and postorder traversals of a binary tree with distinct values, reconstruct the tree.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Same frame, but this time the second catalogue is postorder — children before parents, root recorded last of all.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So the root is at the END. Consume the postorder list from the back and it behaves exactly like preorder consumed from the front.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Three is last, so three is the root. Then inorder splits as before: 9 on the left, 15, 20, 7 on the right.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: But there's a catch. Reading backwards, the next value after the root is 20 — which is the RIGHT subtree's root, not the left's.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is the one detail that separates this from its sibling problem: build the right subtree BEFORE the left, or the pointer into the postorder list falls out of step.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Everything else is identical — the inorder index map, the recursive split, the linear total.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So knowing one of these two really is knowing both, as long as you notice which direction you're consuming from.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And that is the useful habit: when a problem looks like one you know, find the single axis it differs on rather than starting over.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Building the left subtree first, which consumes postorder entries that belong to the right subtree. The result is a plausible tree with the wrong shape rather than a crash.

108.title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array sorted in ascending order, build a height-balanced binary search tree from it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The island was cut in half and every research log survived — sorted, in one long line. Now it has to be rebuilt as a search tree, and the tree must be BALANCED, or looking anything up will be as slow as reading the line itself.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Just insert them one by one? That's the obvious thing.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And it produces the worst tree possible. Inserting sorted values means every new value is larger than everything before it, so it hangs off the right, forever. You would build a linked list wearing a tree's clothes.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So which value should be the root?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The middle one. It is the only choice that leaves exactly as many logs on the left as on the right — and 'balanced' is precisely the claim that the two sides are the same size.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Then the left half is its own sorted line, so the same rule applies to it. Take ITS middle as the left child.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And the right half likewise. The problem is the same problem at a smaller size, which is the whole shape of divide and conquer — split, solve both halves independently, attach.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And the search-tree ordering comes free! Everything left of the middle is smaller, everything right is larger, at every level. The sorted line was doing that work all along.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Note what the recursion should pass around: index bounds, not copies of the array. Slicing at every level would turn a linear build into an n-log-n one for no reason at all.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: With an even number of logs there are two middles. Does it matter which we pick?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Not for correctness — either produces a valid, balanced tree. It changes which tree you get, so a judge comparing against one exact answer may care. Say so out loud rather than guessing.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Inserting the values one at a time, which builds a degenerate chain of height n — the exact opposite of what was asked. Also, slicing sub-arrays rather than passing lo/hi indices quietly adds a log factor.

112.title: Path Sum
112.epTitle: The Route That Spends Exactly Enough

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the root of a binary tree and a target sum, determine whether any root-to-leaf path's values add up to exactly that sum.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The route through the city costs something at every crossing, and we need to know whether any route from the gate to a dead end spends exactly twenty-two.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Carry the remaining budget down instead of the total spent. At each crossing, subtract its cost and hand the rest to the children.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Twenty-two minus five is seventeen. Minus four is thirteen. Minus eleven is two. And the leaf costs exactly two.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The test happens only at a LEAF — a node with no children at all. Reaching zero halfway down means nothing, because the path is not finished.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And a node with one child isn't a leaf, even though it feels like the end of that side.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is where most wrong answers come from. Test for BOTH children being absent, not either — and never treat a null child as a zero-cost leaf, or an empty side will fabricate a path.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The answer is an OR across the two children — either side finding a route is enough.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And negative values are allowed, so you cannot prune when the budget goes below zero. Without that guarantee, an obvious optimisation becomes a bug.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Treating a node with one child as a leaf, or treating a null child as a valid endpoint — both invent paths that do not exist. And pruning on a negative remainder, which is wrong when negative values are allowed.

114.title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Flatten a binary tree into a linked list in place, using the right pointers, in preorder. Every left pointer must end up null.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The frame has to be laid out flat along the dock, in the order you would meet the timbers walking the tree — root, then everything left, then everything right.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Collect the preorder into a list and then re-link? That works, but it needs a whole list of nodes.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is an in-place version with no extra structure. For each node that has a left subtree, find the RIGHTMOST node of that subtree — the last timber you would meet walking it.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And attach the current right subtree onto that tail, because in preorder the right subtree comes immediately after everything on the left.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then move the whole left subtree over to the right pointer, and set the left pointer to null. Advance to the new right and repeat.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So the tree unrolls itself one node at a time, and nothing is ever stored.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Constant space, and linear time — each node is visited once as the current node and at most once while searching for a tail.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Setting the left pointers to null isn't optional either. The problem says the result must be a proper list.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting to null the left pointers, which leaves a tree rather than a list. And attaching the right subtree to the left subtree's root instead of to its rightmost node.

117.title: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node II
117.epTitle: Stringing a Rope Along Each Deck

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a binary tree where each node has an extra next pointer, set each next pointer to the node immediately to its right on the same level, or null if there is none. The tree need not be perfect.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Every deck of the shipyard needs a guide rope running left to right, joining each platform to the one beside it. Some decks have gaps — the tree isn't perfect.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Level-order traversal with a queue would do it — snapshot the level, link them in order.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: It would, at O of width memory. But there is a version with none at all, and it is a lovely idea: once a level has been strung, that level IS a linked list you can walk.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So we use the rope we just tied to walk along and tie the next one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Walk the current level through its next pointers, and for each node hang its children onto a growing list for the level below. A dummy head makes that list painless.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And gaps don't matter — we only ever attach children that exist, so the next level's rope skips the holes automatically.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is exactly why the perfect-tree version of this problem is easier: there, a node's left child always connects to its right child, and no walking is needed.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Using the structure you have just built as the scaffolding for the next piece. That's a genuinely satisfying trick.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Assuming a node's right child follows its left child, which only holds for a perfect tree. With gaps, the next node on the level below may be several parents away.

120.title: Triangle
120.epTitle: The Descent Down the Stone Pyramid

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a triangle array, return the minimum path sum from top to bottom. At each step you may move to either of the two adjacent numbers on the row below.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The pyramid narrows to a single stone at the top and widens as it falls. From any stone you may only drop to the two directly beneath it, and we want the cheapest way down.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Try every route? Each level doubles them. Twenty levels is a million paths.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Work upward instead. For a stone on the bottom row, the cheapest descent is just its own cost. For any stone above, it is its own cost plus the cheaper of the two stones beneath it.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So each stone is answered once, using two answers already computed. No route is ever walked twice.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Going bottom-up also means there is no separate answer to collect at the end — the top stone's value IS the answer, because every path starts there.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Top-down would work too, but then you'd have to scan the whole bottom row for the smallest at the end.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And each row only ever needs the row below it, so one array of the triangle's width is enough. Overwrite it in place, working upward.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: O of n squared time for the stones, O of n space instead of a whole triangle of them.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Choosing the direction so that the answer lands in one place, rather than needing a search afterwards, is a small habit that simplifies a lot of these.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Enumerating paths, which is exponential. And with the rolling-array version, iterating the row in the wrong direction so that a value is read after it has already been overwritten.

121.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given daily prices, find the maximum profit from a single buy followed by a single later sell. If no profit is possible, return 0.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: One purchase, one sale, and the sale must come after the purchase. What is the most we can make on these readings?

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Compare every buy day against every sell day after it? That's every pair again.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Fix the sell day instead, and ask what you need to know about the past. Only one thing: the cheapest price seen before it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So one walk forward carrying two numbers. Update the minimum, and test today's price against it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Seven sets the minimum. One replaces it. Five gives a profit of four. Three gives two. Six gives five — the best. Four gives three.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Why track the minimum rather than the maximum?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Because the buy must come FIRST. Tracking the maximum so far would let you sell before you bought — and on a falling market it would report a profit that is impossible.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And on a market that only falls, the answer is zero. We are allowed to do nothing at all.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Tracking the maximum price so far instead of the minimum, which permits selling before buying. And returning a negative number on a falling market — doing nothing is allowed, so the floor is zero.

122.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
122.epTitle: Trade as Often as the Tide Turns

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given daily prices, maximise profit with unlimited transactions. You may hold at most one unit at a time, and may buy and sell on the same day.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The limit is gone — we may trade as often as we like, so long as we never hold two lots at once.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Find every trough and every peak, pair them up, add the gains? Sounds fiddly to get right at the edges.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is a far simpler equivalent. Buying at a trough and selling at a peak earns exactly the same as buying and selling on every single day of the rise.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Because the intermediate buys and sells cancel out. So we can just add up every day-to-day increase and ignore the peaks entirely.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One to five is four. Three to six is three. Seven in total — and I never had to identify a single peak or trough.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The greedy is correct here because every rise is independent — capturing one never prevents capturing another. That is exactly the property the single-transaction version lacked.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And a falling day contributes nothing, because we simply do not hold anything through it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Add a transaction fee, though, and the argument collapses — a tiny rise might not cover the fee, so the decomposition stops being free. Know why the greedy works, not just that it does.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Assuming this greedy survives added constraints. With a transaction fee, or a cooldown, or a transaction limit, the decomposition is no longer free and the problem becomes a state-machine DP.

123.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given daily prices, find the maximum profit from at most two transactions. You must sell before buying again.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Two trading voyages, no more — and the first cargo must be sold before the second is bought. Maximise the total.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Split the days at every possible point, run the single-transaction algorithm on each side, and take the best split?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Correct, and a good first answer — precompute the best profit for every prefix and every suffix, then combine. Linear time, linear space.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: That works, but it walks the prices three times and keeps two whole arrays. Is there something tighter?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Track four running states as you walk the days once: the best position after buying once, after selling once, after buying twice, and after selling twice.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And each state is built from the one before it. Buying the second cargo spends whatever the first sale earned.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Exactly — buy2 is the best of 'keep the previous buy2' and 'sell1's profit minus today's price'. The states chain, and updating them in order within a single day is perfectly safe here.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Four numbers, one pass, constant space. That's elegant.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And it generalises: k transactions means two k states. Which is precisely the next problem, and why this one is worth understanding as a state machine rather than as a trick.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Assuming two disjoint applications of the single-transaction greedy can be found independently — they interact, since the second buy is constrained by the first sale. Also, "at most two" allows zero or one, so all profits start at zero.

124.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
124.epTitle: The Longest Beam in the Whole Frame

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: A path is any sequence of nodes joined by edges, appearing at most once each, and it need not pass through the root. Return the maximum sum of any path.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The strongest beam in the frame — but a beam can run up one branch, across a joint, and back down another. It doesn't have to pass through the keel at all.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which forces two different quantities at every joint, and confusing them is the whole difficulty of this problem.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Two quantities at one joint? Surely a beam is a beam — what could the difference be?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: What you HAND YOUR PARENT is a beam that can be extended upward — so it may use only one branch, because a parent cannot walk down both. That is the node plus the better of its two sides.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: What you RECORD as a candidate answer may bend at this joint and use BOTH sides — node plus left plus right. That beam is complete; it can never be extended.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Fifteen plus twenty plus seven is forty-two, bending at the twenty. And what twenty hands upward is only thirty-five.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And a branch that would weaken the beam?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Clamp it to zero — a harmful branch is simply not taken. But the recorded answer must still allow a single node, or an all-negative tree returns zero instead of its least bad node.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: One value to propagate, another to record. Once you separate those, the code is six lines.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Returning the bent path to the parent, which lets a parent walk down both branches of a child — an impossible path. And initialising the best to zero, which is wrong on an all-negative tree.

125.title: Valid Palindrome
125.epTitle: The Lighthouse That Reads Both Ways

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a string, decide whether it reads the same forwards and backwards once you ignore case and every character that is not a letter or digit.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: The twin lighthouses at the Cape carry the same inscription — but one is meant to be read from the left and the other from the right. If the words truly match in both directions, the passage opens.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So copy the inscription, reverse the copy, compare. Done. ...Although that means carrying a whole second inscription, and some of these run for hundreds of letters.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Don't copy it. Stand one reader at each end and walk them toward each other. If every pair they meet matches, it reads both ways. The moment one pair disagrees, it does not.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: But the stonemason carved punctuation and spaces into it, and mixed his capitals. Those were never part of the inscription — they are decoration.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Then each reader skips anything that isn't a letter or a digit before it compares, and lowercases what it finds. Decoration is walked past, never compared.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: 'A' against 'a' — same letter once you ignore the case. Skip the comma, skip the colon. Then 'm' against 'm'. They meet in the middle with nothing left to disagree about.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: One walk of the inscription, no second copy. Each reader only ever moves inward, so together they cover the stone exactly once.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: There is one stone on this cape carved with nothing but punctuation. What happens then? Yohohoho — a reader that only knows how to skip will walk straight past the other one and off the end of the world!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: So every skip is bounded by the other reader. Skip while there's still something between us — never past it. And a stone with no letters at all reads the same both ways by default.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: The inner skip loops need the left < right guard. Without it, an input like ".,;" runs a pointer off the end. Odd-length strings need no special case — the pointers simply meet on the middle character and stop.

127.title: Word Ladder
127.epTitle: The Ladder Out of Level Six

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given beginWord, endWord and a word list, return the number of words in the shortest transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord, changing one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in the list. Return 0 if none exists.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The gate codes change one letter at a time, and every code along the way has to be a real word from the guard's book. We're on 'hit' and we need 'cog'.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The same graph as the gene bank, in a different costume. Words are nodes, one-letter changes are edges, everything costs one step — breadth-first search, and the first arrival is the shortest ladder.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: But this book has thirty thousand words. Comparing every word against every other word to find the edges is nine hundred million comparisons before we even start searching.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So we never build the edge list. Bucket the words by pattern instead: 'hot' files under '*ot', 'h*t' and 'ho*'. Any two words sharing a bucket differ by exactly one letter.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So from 'hit' I look up 'h*t' and out falls 'hot', without touching a single unrelated word.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: From 'hot': '*ot' gives 'dot' and 'lot'. Both go in the queue at distance three.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: From 'dot': 'do*' gives 'dog'. From 'dog': '*og' gives 'cog'. Five words in the ladder, counting both ends.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The count is the number of WORDS, not the number of changes. Four changes, five words. That off-by-one has cost people whole interviews.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Once a bucket has been used, empty it. Every word in it has already been reached at this distance or a shorter one, so revisiting can only produce a longer ladder.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And if 'cog' had never been in the book at all, no amount of searching would find it — the answer is zero, not 'nearly'.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: If they push you further, search from both ends at once and stop when the two frontiers touch. The frontier grows exponentially with depth, so halving the depth is close to taking a square root of the work.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Returning the number of transformations instead of the number of words — the answer counts both endpoints. Also: if endWord is not in the list, the answer is 0 regardless of how close it is.

128.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
128.epTitle: The Longest Chain in the Log Pose Ruins

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an unsorted array of integers, find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (numbers that increase by exactly one with no gaps between them) that appears anywhere in the array, in O(n) time.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The Log Pose lists six island coordinates in whatever order the current dropped them in — 100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2 — and somewhere in that mess is the longest unbroken CHAIN of islands, each exactly one degree east of the last!

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: Easy! Just line them up smallest to biggest and walk the line!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Sorting works, Luffy, but it costs extra time just to line them up. There's a faster way: drop every coordinate into a set for instant checking, then only START walking a chain from an island that has NO island directly to its west — because that means nothing shorter completes it. It has to be a true beginning.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Island 100 — is 99 anywhere on the list? No. So 100 begins a chain. Walk east: is 101 on the list? No. Chain length one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Island 4 — is 3 on the list? Yes. Then 4 can never be a chain's start, only its middle — skip it without walking anywhere.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Island 200 — is 199 on the list? No, another true start. Walk east: 201 isn't there either. Chain length one, no better than before.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Island 1 — is 0 on the list? No! A true start. Walk east: 2 is there, 3 is there, 4 is there, 5 is not. That chain runs four islands deep.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Island 3 and island 2 each have a western neighbor already on the list, so they were never chain starts at all — just the middle of the chain we already counted, from island 1.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Four islands, one look each. That's the longest run: 1, 2, 3, 4.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! And we never even had to sort the map!

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Trying to walk a chain from EVERY number instead of only from numbers with no left neighbor (num - 1) in the set. Skipping that check turns the algorithm back into O(n^2) in the worst case, e.g. a fully consecutive array re-walks the same shrinking chain starting from every single element.

129.title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
129.epTitle: Every Serial Number on the Hull

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Each root-to-leaf path spells a number, one digit per node. Return the total of all such numbers.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Every plate on the hull carries a digit, and each route from the keel to an edge spells out a serial number. Iceberg wants them all added up.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Build the number as you descend rather than collecting digits and assembling at the end. Each step down multiplies the running number by ten and adds this node's digit.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So arriving at a leaf, the running number IS that path's serial. Twelve on one side, thirteen on the other.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And the total is the sum of what the two children report. A node with one child reports only that side — the absent side contributes nothing, not a zero-length number.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Which is the trap again. If a null child returned the running number, a node with one child would count its serial twice.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So a null child returns zero, and the leaf test is once more 'both children absent'. Twenty-five in total.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Carrying the value down and summing the results back up — information flowing both ways through the same recursion.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That pairing — a parameter descending, a return value ascending — is the shape of most tree problems worth the name.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Returning the running number from a null child, which double-counts every node that has exactly one child. And rebuilding the number from a digit list at each leaf, which is O(depth) extra work per path for no benefit.

130.title: Surrounded Regions
130.epTitle: The Bubbles That Touch the Sky

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an m x n board of X and O, capture every region of O that is entirely surrounded by X. A region is not captured if any of its cells touches the border.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The coating bubbles on the grove: any bubble touching open air survives, and any bubble sealed in on all sides gets popped by the resin. We need to know which is which.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So for each bubble, check whether its whole region reaches the edge? That means flood-filling every region and asking whether any of its cells is on the border.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Correct, but awkward — you have to fill first and decide afterwards, then go back and act. Turn the question around instead. Do not ask 'which regions are sealed'. Ask 'which regions touch the air'.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Start at the border and flood inward! Anything the flood reaches is connected to open air and therefore safe.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Exactly. Walk the four edges, and from every bubble sitting on them, flood into its whole region and mark it. That is one multi-source search, not one per region.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And then everything still unmarked is, by definition, sealed. Pop it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One sweep at the end restores the marked bubbles and captures the rest. Two passes over the board, no per-region bookkeeping at all.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Inverting the question turned a hard property into an easy one. The easy property was the negation of the one they asked about.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: One practical worry: on a big board, does the recursion get too deep?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: It can. A region spanning the whole board makes the depth proportional to its area. Say so, and offer the iterative version with an explicit stack — or breadth-first, which has the same effect.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Flood-filling each region and then deciding, which needs per-region state and a second visit. Also: mark survivors with a temporary character and restore them at the end, or you cannot tell a survivor from an unvisited cell.

133.title: Clone Graph
133.epTitle: The Copy That Points at Itself

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a reference to a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the whole graph. Each node holds a value and a list of its neighbours.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The Auction House's guest network has to be duplicated exactly — every node, every link — without sharing a single object with the original.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Walk it and copy each node as I meet it. But the links go both ways — node one points at two, and two points back at one. I'd copy one, then two, then follow two's link back to one and copy it again. Forever.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So keep a visited set, like any graph walk.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: A visited set stops the loop, but it leaves you stuck. When you meet node one for the second time, you need to attach ITS COPY to node two's copy — and a set of booleans cannot tell you where that copy is.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So the visited structure has to be a map. Original node to its clone. It does both jobs at once — it remembers what we've seen AND where the copy lives.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The recursion then reads cleanly. Arrive at a node: if it is already in the map, return its clone and stop. Otherwise create the clone, record it in the map BEFORE recursing, then clone each neighbour and attach.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Before recursing. That's the part I'd get wrong — if you record it after, the cycle comes back round to a node that isn't in the map yet and off you go again.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Exactly. The map entry must exist before any neighbour is explored. That single ordering is what makes cycles safe rather than fatal.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And a graph of one node with no links at all? Or an empty reference?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Both worth handling explicitly — null in, null out; and an isolated node clones to an isolated node with an empty neighbour list. The problem gives you both, so they will be in the tests.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Using a plain visited set, which prevents infinite recursion but leaves you unable to attach the right clone on a revisit. And recording the clone after exploring neighbours, which reintroduces the infinite recursion it was meant to prevent.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: There are n gas stations arranged in a circle. Station i has gas[i] fuel, and it costs cost[i] fuel to travel from station i to the next station. Starting with an empty tank at one station, find the starting station index that lets you complete the entire circuit exactly once (guaranteed to be unique if a solution exists), or return -1 if no valid starting station exists.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Five gas stations on this ring route. Each one gives you a set amount of fuel, but it costs a set amount to reach the NEXT station. We start with an empty tank — which station lets us make the full loop without ever running dry?

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: Just try starting at every station and see which one works?

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: That works, but it is slow to redo the whole loop five separate times. Here's the shortcut: if total gas across the whole route is at least total cost, SOME starting station must work. Walk the loop once, tracking the running tank from a candidate start — the moment the tank goes negative, none of the stations we just tried could have been the true start, so move the candidate to the very next station and reset the tank to zero.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Station 0: gain 1, spend 3, net -2. Tank drops to -2 — negative! Station 0 can't be the start. Try station 1 next, tank resets to 0.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Station 1: gain 2, spend 4, net -2. Tank drops to -2 again — negative! Move on to station 2, reset.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Station 2: gain 3, spend 5, net -2. Negative again! Move on to station 3, reset.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Station 3: gain 4, spend 1, net +3. Tank climbs to 3 — positive, keep station 3 as our candidate and keep going.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Station 4: gain 5, spend 2, net +3. Tank climbs to 6 — still positive, and that was the last station on the loop.

clips.speaker: robin
