clips.line: Total gas (1+2+3+4+5 = 15) equals total cost (3+4+5+1+2 = 15), so a valid start does exist — and since the tank never went negative again after we locked in station 3, that's the one.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Fill up at station 3 and we sail the whole loop without running dry!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Every time the tank goes negative, it wasn't the driver's fault — it was every station tried so far. Wipe the slate, start fresh from the next one.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting to first confirm that total gas ≥ total cost overall — the single-pass trick correctly finds the ONE candidate that never goes negative twice in a row, but if the totals don't balance, no station works at all and the answer must be -1, even though the scan will still "find" a candidate.

135.title: Candy
135.epTitle: Sharing the Sweets Without a Riot

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Children stand in a line with ratings. Each must get at least one sweet, and any child with a higher rating than a neighbour must get more sweets than that neighbour. Return the minimum total.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Every child gets at least one sweet, and any child rated above a neighbour must get strictly more than that neighbour. Use as few sweets as possible.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: There are two constraints pulling in opposite directions — the left neighbour and the right neighbour. Satisfying one can break the other.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So satisfy them one at a time. Walk left to right giving one extra sweet whenever a child outranks the one on their left. That handles every left-hand constraint and ignores the right.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Then walk right to left doing the same for the right-hand neighbour.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And take the MAXIMUM of the two demands at each child. The maximum satisfies both, and nothing smaller could satisfy either.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Why doesn't the second pass break what the first one established?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Because it only ever raises a value, and raising a child's count can never violate a left-hand constraint that was already satisfied. Taking the maximum is monotone — that is the whole argument.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Two passes, one array, linear time. And equal ratings impose nothing at all — only a STRICTLY higher rating demands more.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: A single pass, which cannot see a rise that begins after the current child. And giving more sweets on EQUAL ratings — the rule fires only on a strictly higher rating.

136.title: Single Number
136.epTitle: The Last Duelist Standing on Sabaody

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of integers where every number appears exactly twice except for one number that appears exactly once, find that single number. You must do it in linear time and without using extra memory for a counting structure.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Gather round! Five cards on the table at the Sabaody duel ring — and legend says every card has an exact rival among the others, matched down to the bit... except ONE, the Unrivaled Card!

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: With only five cards I could just compare every pair by hand, sure. But if this table had ten thousand cards, checking every pair against every other one would take forever.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is an operation called XOR — it flips a bit where two numbers disagree and leaves it alone where they agree. Two identical numbers XORed together always land on zero.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And zero XORed with anything just gives back that thing unchanged. So if I fold every card into one running total, any card with a rival cancels itself out completely — no matter what order they arrive in.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Card one: 4. Running total was 000, now it is 100.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Card two: 1. Fold it in — total becomes 101.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Card three: 2. Total becomes 111.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Card four: 1 again — its rival! Folding it in flips those same bits right back, so the 1's worth cancels out of the total. New total: 110.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Card five: 2 again — its rival too! Cancel it out the same way. New total: 100.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Every card that had a partner is gone from the total now. Only the 4 never got cancelled.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! The Unrivaled Card is the 4! We never even had to write down which cards we'd already seen!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is the whole trick: one running XOR, one pass, no lookup table needed — the pairs cancel themselves out of existence.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Reaching for a hash-map count of occurrences works but violates the "constant extra space" requirement — the whole point of this pattern is that XOR gives you the same answer with zero extra memory, since a^a=0 and a^0=a for any a.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Every element in the array appears exactly three times except for one, which appears once. Find that element, in linear time and constant extra space.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Every blade in the armoury was struck three times by the same smith — except one, struck once. Find it. And the smiths kept no ledger, so we can't just count.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Count with a hash map, obviously. ...Which they've forbidden. Constant space only.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: In the version where everything appears twice, exclusive-or does it — pairs cancel. But XOR only knows how to count to two. Here we need something that counts to three and resets.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So work one bit position at a time. Across all the numbers, count how many have a one in that position. Every thrice-struck blade contributes three, or none — so the total is a multiple of three, PLUS whatever the lone blade contributes.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: So take that count modulo three. What's left in each position is exactly the lone blade's bit.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: That's thirty-two passes over the array, one per bit. Still linear, and the space is a single counter. I'd be happy handing that in.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: It is the right answer to give first. There is a sharper one: keep two accumulators, 'seen once' and 'seen twice', and update both with bit operations so that a bit appearing a third time is cleared from both at once.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: A counter that counts to three across every bit position simultaneously, in two registers.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One warning for languages with fixed-width signed integers: if the lone blade is negative, the modulo-three reconstruction needs a sign fix-up at the end. Python's unbounded integers hide that, and the hiding is itself worth knowing about.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Reaching for XOR out of habit — it cancels pairs, not triples, and returns nonsense here. In fixed-width signed languages, the per-bit reconstruction needs sign extension when the answer is negative.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Deep copy a linked list where each node has a next pointer and a random pointer that may point to any node in the list, or to null.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The vine has two kinds of link: one to the next vine along, and one that can reach out to any vine at all — including backwards, or to itself. We need a complete duplicate that shares nothing with the original.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Copy the nodes in one pass, then go back and fix the random pointers. But when I copy A's random pointer, the node it points at might not exist yet.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So build them all first, then wire. And to wire, you need to know which copy corresponds to which original — that is a map from original node to its clone.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: First pass makes every clone and records the pairing. Second pass sets each clone's next and random by looking up the original's targets in the map.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And the interviewer immediately asks for constant space.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then weave the clones INTO the original list. After each original node, insert its copy. Now every clone sits directly behind its original — the map is the list itself.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So a clone's random pointer is whatever its original's random points at, plus one step. No lookup needed.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then unweave: restore the original list's next pointers and extract the clone chain. Three passes, no extra structure at all.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The unweaving is where people leave the original list mangled, isn't it.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Wiring random pointers during the first pass, when the target clone may not exist yet. In the interleaved version, forgetting to restore the original list's next pointers on the way out.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a string s and a dictionary of words, decide whether s can be segmented into a sequence of one or more dictionary words. A word may be reused any number of times.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The transmission came through with every space stripped out — one unbroken run of letters. Vegapunk's dictionary is right here, but where do the cuts go?

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Try every possible set of cuts? For a message this long that's two to the power of everything. We'd be here until the next Reverie.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then let's not ask about the whole message at once. Ask a much smaller question, over and over: can the FIRST i letters be cut cleanly? Write it as a sentence and the code follows from the sentence.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The first zero letters can be cut cleanly — there is nothing there to cut. That is the base case, and it has to be true or nothing else can ever start.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So for each position, I look backwards: is there some earlier position that was already true, where the stretch from there to here is a whole dictionary word?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Position five. Look back to position zero — true — and the letters from zero to five spell 'apple'. Both halves hold, so position five is true.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Position eight. Look back to five — true — and five to eight spells 'pen'. True as well!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And the end, position thirteen: back to eight, which is true, and eight to thirteen spells 'apple'. The whole transmission cuts cleanly.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The clever part is that once a position is settled, it's settled forever. We never re-derive it, no matter how many later positions ask about it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is the whole of dynamic programming. And note the direction of the check — a position becomes true only if some EARLIER true position plus one word reaches it. A word alone is never enough.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: There's a trap, isn't there. If I check 'is any dictionary word a prefix of the rest' without asking whether where I'm standing is reachable, I'd accept nonsense.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Precisely. Both halves must hold: reachable, and then a word. One without the other proves nothing.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Getting dp[0] wrong. It must be true — the empty prefix is trivially segmentable — or nothing downstream can ever become true. The other classic is checking only whether a word fits at position i without requiring i itself to be reachable.

141.title: Linked List Cycle
141.epTitle: The Fog That Never Lets Go

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the head of a linked list, determine whether it contains a cycle — some node's "next" pointer leads back to a node already visited — using O(1) extra space.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: Ships go into the Florian Triangle's fog and just... never come back out, right? Let's find out if our OWN charted course is one of those loops before we sail it for real.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: I'll walk the route at normal speed, one waypoint per minute. You go Gear Second — two waypoints a minute. If the course loops, you'll catch up to me eventually. If it doesn't, you just sail off the edge of the chart and we're done.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: One minute in: I'm already two waypoints ahead, at C. You're only at B.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Two minutes: I've reached C. You've raced ahead to E — through D. If this route were a straight line to open sea, you'd just keep pulling away from me forever.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: But it's NOT a straight line — past E, the fog loops back to C! So my next two steps put me right back at D... and you're walking into D too!

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: We're standing on the same waypoint. The fast route lapped the slow one — that ONLY happens if the course loops. It's the Florian Triangle, alright. We chart around it.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI, no ghost ship's getting the Sunny! And I didn't even need a map of every waypoint we'd already visited — just two speeds!

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Advancing the fast pointer without checking `fast.next` first — on a list with no cycle, fast reaches the end and `fast.next.next` crashes on None unless both `fast` and `fast.next` are checked every iteration.

146.title: LRU Cache
146.epTitle: The Dial That Forgets the Oldest Sound

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Design a cache with a fixed capacity supporting get and put in O(1) average time. When it is full, evict the least recently used entry.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The Tone Dial holds only so many sounds. Recording a new one when it is full overwrites whichever sound has gone longest without being played.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So we need to find a sound instantly by name, AND know which one is stalest. Those feel like two different structures.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: They are, and the answer is to keep both. A hash map gives instant lookup by key. A doubly linked list keeps the entries in order of use, most recent at the front.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And the map doesn't store the value — it stores the NODE, so we can reach straight into the middle of the list.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is what makes everything constant time. On a get, unlink the node from wherever it sits and move it to the front. Unlinking needs its neighbours — which is exactly why the list must be DOUBLY linked.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: With a singly linked list you'd have to walk from the head to find the predecessor. Linear, every single time.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: On a put over capacity, take the node at the back, remove it from the list, and — the step people forget — delete its key from the map too. Otherwise the map keeps growing forever.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Sentinel nodes at both ends again, so no insertion or removal ever needs to ask whether it is at an edge.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Two structures, each covering the other's weakness. That pairing — a map for lookup and something else for order — is one of the most reusable designs there is.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Using a singly linked list, which makes unlinking O(n) because the predecessor must be found. And evicting from the list without deleting the key from the map, which leaks entries and breaks later lookups.

148.title: Sort List
148.epTitle: Sorting a Chain You Cannot Index

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the head of a linked list, return it sorted in ascending order, in O(n log n) time and using constant extra space beyond the recursion.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The chain has to be sorted, and we can't lift it into a bucket first — captain's orders. Quicksort, then?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Quicksort needs to reach into the middle of the data at will, and a chain has no middle you can reach — only a middle you can walk to. It degrades badly here.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: What about a heap? Or just reading the values into an array, sorting, and writing them back?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Both work. Both spend O(n) extra space, which is exactly what we were told not to spend. Merge sort is the one that fits a chain: it never needs to jump anywhere.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Splitting: send one runner at single speed and one at double. When the fast one reaches the end, the slow one is standing on the middle — and we cut the chain there.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Cut it properly, though. If we don't set the first half's last link to nothing, both halves still point into each other and the recursion never bottoms out.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Sever the link, then sort each half. Four and two becomes two, four. One and three becomes one, three.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And now the merge — which is where the actual work is. Two sorted chains, walk both fronts, always take the smaller.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: One, then two, then three, then four. And it's all pointer rewiring — no new nodes made, nothing copied.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: A dummy head makes the merge painless: every node then has a predecessor, so there is no special case for whichever list contributes the first element.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So the honest answer on space is 'constant, apart from the log-n recursion stack'. Which they will absolutely ask about.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Failing to sever the link between the two halves before recursing, which leaves both halves sharing nodes and recursing forever. Also, with two nodes, a fast/slow split must not return the whole list as one half or the recursion never shrinks.

149.title: Max Points on a Line
149.epTitle: The Arrows That Share One Flight

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of points on a plane, return the maximum number of points that lie on the same straight line.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Every arrow that landed is marked on the map. How many of them were loosed along the same line of flight?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: A line is fixed by two points, so fix one arrow and look at the direction to every other. Arrows sharing a direction from that one all lie on one line through it.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So for each arrow, tally the directions to all the others and take the biggest tally. That's n times n — fine, n is small here.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The difficulty is the KEY. Using the slope as a decimal invites floating-point error — two genuinely collinear arrows can hash to different values because one division rounded differently.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So keep it as a fraction. The rise and the run, as a pair of whole numbers.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Reduced by their greatest common divisor, and with the sign normalised — otherwise two over four, one over two, and minus one over minus two all name the same direction under three different keys.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Three arrows on the diagonal all give a reduced direction of one over one. Tally three.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Vertical lines have zero run, which as a fraction would divide by zero — but as a reduced PAIR it is simply one over zero, and needs no special case at all.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Choosing the key so the awkward cases disappear, rather than branching around them. That keeps coming up.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Using a floating-point slope, where rounding makes collinear points disagree. And forgetting to normalise the sign of the reduced fraction, which splits one direction across several keys.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Evaluate an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation, where each operator follows its two operands.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The old battle log writes the operation AFTER the two things it acts on. Two, one, add. Then three, multiply. No brackets anywhere.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is why there are no brackets — the order is unambiguous without them. Read left to right: a number goes onto a stack, and an operator takes the top two, combines them, and pushes the result back.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Push two. Push one. Then add — pop both, push three. Then push three. Then multiply — pop both, push nine.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One value left at the end, and that's the answer. Neat.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is one trap and it is entirely about order. The SECOND value you pop is the LEFT operand. Addition and multiplication hide the mistake completely; subtraction and division expose it at once.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Because the left operand went on first, so it's underneath. Pop b, then pop a, then compute a minus b.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And division here truncates toward zero, which is not the same as flooring. Minus seven divided by two is minus three, not minus four — a distinction Python's own operator gets 'wrong' for this problem.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So I have to write the truncation myself rather than reach for the built-in.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: In Python, yes — int(a / b) truncates, while a // b floors. Two characters apart, and only wrong on negative results, which is exactly the kind of test a judge includes.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Computing b - a instead of a - b, which is invisible under addition and multiplication. And using floor division for negative results when the problem specifies truncation toward zero.

151.title: Reverse Words in a String
151.epTitle: The Order of the Message, Turned Around

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Reverse the order of the words in a string. Words are separated by one or more spaces; the result must have single spaces and no leading or trailing space.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The message has to be read back with its words in reverse order — and the transcription is full of stray spaces that must not survive.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Split on whitespace, reverse the list, join with single spaces. Three operations and the spacing is handled for free.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is the right answer in most languages, and worth saying plainly. A whitespace split with no argument collapses runs of spaces and drops the empty pieces automatically.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And if they ask for it in place, on a character array?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then it is the reversal trick again. Reverse the entire string, which puts the words in the right order but each one backwards. Then reverse each word individually to straighten it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Exactly the same double-reversal as rotating an array. Two applications of one idea.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Plus a compaction pass to squeeze the extra spaces out, which is the fiddly part and the reason the split version is preferable when it is allowed.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Know both, offer the simple one, and have the in-place version ready for the follow-up.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Splitting on a single space rather than on whitespace runs, which produces empty strings between repeated spaces. And leaving a leading or trailing space in the joined result.

153.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: An array that was once sorted in ascending order has been rotated at some unknown pivot, with no duplicate values. Find the minimum element in O(log n) time.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Okay, I MIGHT have tripped into the garden sundial this morning. The seven hour-stones used to run smallest to biggest all the way around — now they're spun to some unknown point. There's exactly one smallest stone hiding in the ring. Find it, and we know exactly how far it turned.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Can't we just look at all seven stones and see which one is smallest?

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: With seven, sure. With seven hundred, we'd be here all night. It's still HALF sorted at any split — same trick as always: cut it in half and figure out which half is hiding the smallest one.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Middle stone, index three: marked seven. Compare it to the LAST stone in range, index six, marked two. Seven is bigger than two — stones only ever drop from big back to small once, at the turnover point, and that hasn't happened yet by index three. So the smallest stone is still ahead, past the middle.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Throw away index zero through three entirely. Search only four through six.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: New middle: index five, marked one. Compare to the last stone in THIS range, index six, marked two. One is smaller — the turnover already happened at or before index five, so the smallest is index five or something before it, never past it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Search shrinks to index four through five.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Middle now: index four, marked zero. Compare to the last stone in range, index five, marked one. Zero is smaller — same logic. The smallest is index four or before, never past it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: That shrinks the range to exactly one stone: index four.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One stone left in range means we're done — a range of exactly one is always, trivially, its own smallest. Stone marked zero it is.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI, so the sundial used to start counting right THERE, and Usopp spun it four stones too far!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Compare the middle to the edge of your range, not to some target. Bigger than the edge, the drop's still ahead — go right. Smaller or equal, the drop already happened — stay left, keep the middle in play.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Comparing the middle stone against the FIRST stone in range instead of the LAST one. Comparing mid to the range's left edge tells you whether the rotation point is inside the left half, but it doesn't cleanly tell you whether to keep or discard the middle itself — comparing mid to the right edge (hi) lets you always shrink with `hi = mid` (keeping mid as a live candidate) instead of accidentally skipping past the true minimum.

155.title: Min Stack
155.epTitle: The Scale That Remembers Its Lightest

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Design a stack supporting push, pop, top and retrieving the minimum element, all in constant time.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The treasure scale stacks weights, and at any moment we need the LIGHTEST one currently on it — instantly, not by looking through the pile.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Keep a variable holding the smallest. Update it on every push. Easy.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Until the smallest is popped off. Then what does that variable become? You would have to scan the whole pile to find out — and that is linear, not constant.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So one variable can't survive a pop, because it holds no history.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then store the minimum AS OF each push, alongside the value. Push three: the minimum so far is three. Push one: the minimum so far is one. Push four: still one.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Now popping restores the previous minimum for free — it's sitting right there under the one we removed.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Every operation is constant time, and the price is one extra number per element — O(n) space rather than O(1). That trade is the answer, and stating it is part of the answer.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: You could keep a second stack that only grows when a new minimum arrives, which saves space when the values mostly increase.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: You can — but then pop must compare before removing from it, and equal values need care or you drop a minimum that is still on the scale. The paired version is harder to get wrong.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Keeping one min variable and trying to repair it on pop, which is O(n). In the two-stack variant, using a strict < when pushing minima drops a duplicate minimum that is still in the stack.

162.title: Find Peak Element
162.epTitle: Climbing the Back of the Elephant

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: A peak is an element strictly greater than its neighbours. Given an array where neighbouring values are never equal, return the index of any peak in O(log n) time. Treat out-of-bounds neighbours as negative infinity.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Zunesha's back rises and falls. We need any spot higher than both its neighbours — and the edges count as dropping off into the sea.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Just walk along until it stops rising. That's linear, and they've asked for logarithmic. But the array isn't sorted — how can we possibly halve it?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Sortedness was never the requirement. What binary search needs is a rule that lets you discard half with certainty. And here there is one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Stand anywhere. If the ground to your right is higher, then walking right you must eventually reach a peak — either it keeps rising to the very end, which makes the last spot a peak, or it turns over somewhere.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So the whole left half can be thrown away — not because there's no peak there, but because we're guaranteed one on the right and we only need any peak.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And symmetrically, if the ground to the right is lower, then a peak lies at or to the left of where you stand. One comparison, half the mountain gone.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Middle of seven is position three, value 3. To its right is 5 — higher. Discard the left half. Then middle of the rest, value 6, and to its right is 4 — lower. Keep the left. Converges on position five.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The condition that no two neighbours are equal is doing real work here, isn't it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: It is what makes the comparison decisive. On a plateau neither direction is guaranteed, and the problem becomes genuinely linear — a constraint that looks decorative and is in fact the whole licence.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Comparing against both neighbours and handling the edges separately, which is fiddly. Comparing nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1] alone is sufficient, provided hi starts at n − 1 so mid + 1 is always in range.

167.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
167.epTitle: The Keel of the Thousand Sunny

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a list of numbers already sorted in ascending order and a target value, return the 1-indexed positions of the two numbers that add up to the target exactly, using O(1) extra space.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Iceburg's blueprint says the crossbeam brace needs two salvaged plates that weigh EXACTLY 25 stone together. Over or under and the whole frame's stress rating is wrong.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Six plates on the rack, already sorted lightest to heaviest. We are NOT weighing every possible pair — that's fifteen trips up this ladder.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Lightest plate and heaviest plate, together: 4 plus 20 is 24. One short. The only honest fix is the light end giving us more.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Then I step in from the light end — plate 7 instead of plate 4.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: 7 plus 20 is 27 — now we're over. Heavy end steps down.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: 7 plus 16 is 23 — short again. Light end steps in once more, to plate 9.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: 9 plus 16 is 25. Exact. Plates three and five come off the rack.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And plate 4, plate 20 — never touched again after we stepped past them. Once an end steps inward, it never steps back out. That's the whole trick, Iceburg-san!

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Moving the wrong end: if the sum is too small you must move the LEFT pointer inward (to a bigger value), not the right one. Moving the wrong pointer can step past the only valid pair.

169.title: Majority Element
169.epTitle: The Flag More Than Half the Fleet Flies

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array where one element appears more than n/2 times, return that element. You may assume it always exists.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One flag flies on more than half the fleet. Which one? And Nami has confiscated my notebook, so no tallying.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Sort the fleet and look at the middle ship — the majority flag has to cover the centre. That's n log n and it works.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Correct, and worth saying. But there is a linear method needing exactly two variables: a candidate flag and a count.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: When the count is zero, adopt whatever flag you are looking at. Then add one for every ship flying it and subtract one for every ship that is not.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So it's a duel. Every other flag trades itself one-for-one against the majority flag.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And since the majority holds strictly more than half, it cannot be cancelled out — there simply are not enough other ships. Whatever is standing at the end is the answer.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: It relies on the majority genuinely existing, though. Without that guarantee the survivor could be anything.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So if the guarantee is removed, a second pass counting the candidate confirms it. One extra loop, and the claim becomes honest.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Applying it without the majority guarantee — the survivor is then meaningless and needs a verification pass. And resetting the candidate on every mismatch rather than only when the count reaches zero.

172.title: Factorial Trailing Zeroes
172.epTitle: Counting the Zeros Without Counting the Cups

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an integer n, return the number of trailing zeroes in n factorial.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The feast tally is a factorial — every number up to n multiplied together. We need only the count of trailing zeros, and n runs into the tens of thousands.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Compute the factorial and count the zeros at the end. ...Which overflows before we reach twenty-one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So never compute it. A trailing zero is a factor of ten, and a ten is a two paired with a five. Count the pairs.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And twos are far more plentiful than fives — every second number contributes a two, but only every fifth contributes a five.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So the fives are the scarce resource, and the answer is simply how many factors of five appear across all the numbers up to n.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: n over five, then. For twenty-five that's five fives — but twenty-five is five times five, so it contributes two on its own.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is why you also add n over twenty-five, and n over a hundred and twenty-five, and so on. Each higher power counts the extra fives its multiples carry.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Twenty-five over five is five, plus twenty-five over twenty-five is one. Six zeros. And the loop ends as soon as the divisor exceeds n.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Logarithmic in n, and nothing ever overflows because we never build the number at all. Counting a property instead of computing the object is a move worth remembering.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Returning just n // 5, which misses that 25 contributes two fives, 125 contributes three, and so on. Also, counting twos instead of fives gives an answer that is far too large.

173.title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
173.epTitle: The Foreman Who Calls the Next Number

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Implement an iterator over a BST that returns its values in ascending order, with next() and hasNext() running in average O(1) time and O(h) memory.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The foreman calls out plate numbers in order, one whenever asked — but the whole list is far too big to write out in advance.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So we can't just do an in-order traversal into a list up front. That's O of n memory and it does all the work before the first call.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Instead, keep the traversal PAUSED. A recursive in-order walk uses a call stack; make that stack explicit and you can stop it between any two steps.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: At construction, push the root and every left child down to the smallest. The top of the stack is then the next number to call.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: On each call, pop the top — that is the answer — and if it has a right child, push that child and all of ITS left descendants. The stack always holds the pending ancestors.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Some calls push several nodes and some push none. So how is it O of one?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Amortised. Every node is pushed exactly once and popped exactly once across the entire iteration, so n calls do O of n work in total — an average of one apiece.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And the memory is the stack depth, which is the tree height — not the node count.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Turning recursion into an explicit stack so it can be paused is how every lazy iterator over a nested structure is built. Well worth having in hand.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Flattening the tree into a list in the constructor, which is O(n) memory and violates the stated bound. And forgetting to push the right child's left spine after popping, which skips values.

188.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
188.epTitle: As Many Voyages as the Charter Allows

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given daily prices and an integer k, find the maximum profit from at most k transactions, selling before buying again.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The charter allows k voyages this season. Same rule — sell before you buy again — and we want the most profit the charter permits.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The two-voyage version used four states. This is the same machine with two k of them: for each allowed transaction, a 'holding' state and a 'sold' state.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So walk the days once, and for each day update all k pairs of states in order.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: O of n times k, with O of k memory. The transaction index is the second dimension — that is what makes this a two-dimensional DP even though the prices are a flat list.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And if k is enormous? A charter for a thousand voyages over ten days is not really a limit at all.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Precisely. A transaction needs at least two days, so more than n over two of them can never all be used. Above that threshold the constraint stops binding and the answer is the unlimited version — sum every upward step.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Which also stops us allocating a table of a billion states for a ten-day list.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That guard is the difference between passing and timing out on this problem. Noticing when a parameter stops binding is worth as much as the recurrence itself.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Allocating an O(n · k) table before checking whether k is enormous, which blows memory or time on inputs where k is far larger than the price list. Also, "at most k" allows fewer, so the sold states start at zero.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Rotate an array to the right by k steps, in place, where k is non-negative.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Everyone shifts three posts around the deck, and the last three wrap around to the front. No spare deck to stage them on.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Move the last one to the front, k times? That's k passes over the whole crew.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Three reversals instead. Reverse the entire line — that puts the last k at the front, but backwards. Then reverse the first k to straighten them, and reverse the rest to straighten those.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Three linear passes, no extra deck. And every element ends up exactly where it should.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Why does that work? It looks like a coincidence.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Reversing the whole line reverses each block AND swaps their positions. Reversing each block afterwards undoes the first half of that, leaving only the swap — which is the rotation.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And k can be larger than the crew. Rotating seven people by ten is the same as rotating by three.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So reduce k modulo the length first, or the block boundaries fall outside the array. That one line is where most attempts break.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting k %= n, which sends the block boundary out of range. And rotating left instead of right — reversing the first n−k rather than the first k.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Reverse the bits of a given 32-bit unsigned integer.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Oden's seal is stamped in reverse — the last stroke first, the first stroke last. Thirty-two strokes exactly. We have to produce the mirror of it.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Write it out as a string of ones and zeroes, reverse the string, read it back?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That works and it is honest. But there is a version with no strings at all: pour the strokes from one vessel into another. Take the lowest bit off the source, push it onto the bottom of the result — and the result shifts up each time.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: So each round: shift the result left to make room, or in the source's lowest bit, shift the source right. Thirty-two rounds, exactly.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The first bit taken off the source ends up furthest from the bottom of the result, because it has been shifted left thirty-one more times. That is the reversal, and it costs no memory.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Why exactly thirty-two rounds? If the number is small, the source hits zero early.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And that is the trap. Stopping when the source empties would produce a result that has not been shifted far enough — the leading zeroes are real bits here, and they must be carried through. The width is part of the problem.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: So the loop counts, rather than testing for zero. Fixed width, fixed rounds.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: If they ask you to do better, there is a divide-and-conquer version: swap the two sixteen-bit halves, then the eight-bit quarters within those, then fours, twos and ones. Five masked steps instead of thirty-two.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Ending the loop when the source reaches zero. For n = 1 that gives 1 instead of 0x80000000, because the 31 leading zeroes never get shifted through. Also, in Java use >>>, not >>.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an unsigned integer, count how many of its bits are set to 1 (its "Hamming weight"). Do it without checking all 32 bit positions one by one if you can avoid it.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: n is 1011 in binary — eleven! But how many of these four lanterns are actually lit? I only count two hands' worth of fingers, this is confusing!

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: We could just walk through all 32 bit positions of a real integer and check each one for a 1. It works, but most positions are already zero — that is a lot of wasted checks.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is a shortcut: n AND (n minus 1) always clears out the lowest lit lantern and leaves every other lantern exactly as it was. So we just repeat that and count each clear, until n goes dark.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: n is 1011, n-1 is 1010. AND them together and the lowest lantern — bit0 — snuffs out. Count: 1.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Snuffed.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: n is now 1010, n-1 is 1001. AND them and the next lowest lantern — bit1 — snuffs out. Count: 2.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Snuffed.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: n is now 1000, n-1 is 0111. AND them and the last lantern — bit3 — snuffs out too. Count: 3.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: n's zero now. Nothing left to clear. Three lanterns were lit.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Three! And that middle lantern was never even lit, we didn't waste a single check on it!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is the whole idea: only spend a step for each 1-bit that actually exists, instead of marching past every position whether it is lit or not.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting that `n & (n-1)` only clears the LOWEST set bit, not all bits below it — some people assume it zeroes out everything to the right, which would silently produce a wrong count for numbers with multiple 1-bits.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: You're planning a heist down a street of houses, each holding a known amount of loot. Adjacent houses share a connected alarm system — if you rob two houses next to each other, the alarm trips. Return the maximum total loot you can steal without ever robbing two adjacent houses.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Five houses on this street, holding 2, 7, 9, 3, and 1 thousand Berries. Rob two houses that are next-door neighbors and both alarms scream at once. What's the most we can walk away with?

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: Easy! Just rob all five!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The alarms won't allow that, captain. For each house, we only have two honest choices: skip it and keep whatever was best up to the house before it, or rob it and add its loot to whatever was best up to TWO houses before it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: House 0: nothing before it to conflict with. Best so far: rob it. 2.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: House 1: rob it alone (7) beats keeping house 0's 2. Best so far: 7 — meaning house 0's plan gets replaced.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: House 2: skip it and keep 7, OR rob it plus whatever was best before house 1 (which was house 0's 2): 9 + 2 = 11. 11 beats 7 — rob houses 0 and 2.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: House 3: skip it, keep 11, OR rob it plus the best before house 2 (house 1's 7): 3 + 7 = 10. 11 still wins — skip house 3 entirely.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: House 4: skip it, keep 11, OR rob it plus the best before house 3 (still 11, from houses 0 and 2): 1 + 11 = 12. 12 wins!

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Houses 0, 2, and 4: 2 + 9 + 1 = 12,000 Berries, and not one pair of them is adjacent.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! 12,000 Berries of meat money!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Every house only ever looks two decisions back. No need to keep the whole street in your head.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Comparing a house only against its immediate previous house's best, instead of against 'skip vs. rob + best-before-the-previous-one' — that shortcut misses cases like this one, where the optimal plan skips house 3 entirely because reaching back to house 1 wasn't as good as the run already banked at house 2.

199.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
199.epTitle: The Tower Seen From the Sea

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on its right side. Return the values of the nodes you can see, ordered from top to bottom.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: We're approaching the Tower of Justice from the sea, on the right. From out here you can only see the rightmost window on each floor — everything behind it is hidden.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So we want, for every floor, the window furthest to the right. Do we just keep walking right from the top?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Careful. That works only while the right side keeps going. If a floor has no right-hand room at all, what you see is whatever is furthest right on that floor — which may hang off the left side of the building.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Level five! It hangs under the left tower, but there's nothing to its right on that floor. So from the sea it would be visible — if there were nothing else on that floor.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is why we survey floor by floor rather than following a wall. Take the whole floor at once, and report its last room.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Here is the trick that makes 'a whole floor at once' possible. Put the root in a queue. At the top of each round, the number of rooms waiting in that queue IS the width of the current floor.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So I snapshot that count first, then take exactly that many out — and everything I add while draining belongs to the NEXT floor, not this one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Floor two holds rooms two and three. The last one drained is three — that is what the sea sees. Floor three holds five and four; the last is four.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One, three, four. And if I'd just walked down the right wall I'd have got one, three, four here too — but only because this building happens to be lucky.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Take a tower whose right side stops after two floors while the left side runs on for six. Walking the wall reports two floors. The survey reports six. That is the difference between the two methods.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And if you snapshot the count AFTER you start adding children, the floors bleed into each other and the whole thing quietly falls apart.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Read the width before you start building the next floor. One line, and it is the line the entire family of level-order problems rests on.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Assuming the right side view is "walk right children only". A node with no right sibling anywhere on its level is visible even if it hangs off a left branch. Also, capture the level width before enqueuing children, never during.

200.title: Number of Islands
200.epTitle: The Reef Chart After the Storm

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a 2D grid where each cell is either land (1) or water (0), count the number of islands. An island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically (never diagonally), surrounded by water on every other side.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The great cartographer Usopp presents: the reef chart, redrawn after last night's storm! Every square is either dry land or open sea — but the storm scrambled the shoreline into pieces!

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: But some land squares are right next to each other! Do we count each square as its own tiny island, or do the touching ones count as one big island?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One big island — but only if they touch up, down, left, or right. Diagonal doesn't count. So here's the plan: scan every square once. The moment we find land we haven't charted yet, we flood outward from it, marking every connected land square as the SAME island before we move on.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Top-left corner, (0,0): land, and unmarked. New island! I'll flood outward from here.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Its right neighbor (0,1) is also land — same island, mark it too. Its neighbor below (0,1)'s square, (1,1), is land as well — still the same flood.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: No more unmarked land touches this cluster. That flood is finished — three squares, one island.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Keep scanning! (0,2) sea, skip. (1,0) sea, skip. (1,2) sea, skip. (2,0) and (2,1), both sea, skip and skip!

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Bottom-right corner, (2,2) — land, and it's never been touched by either flood! That has to be a brand new island, all on its own.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Correct — nothing connects to it. Its own island.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Two islands, and we only ever floated over each square ONE time! Perfect for exploring — and for lunch, if either one has meat!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Scan once. Flood once per new landmass. Never re-check a square that's already been claimed. That's the whole technique.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting to mark a land cell as visited the MOMENT it's added to the flood (not after it's fully processed) — without that, a cell can be re-queued by two different neighbors and get double-counted or cause infinite recursion.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given two integers left and right, return the bitwise AND of every number in the inclusive range [left, right].

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Every banner from the fifth to the seventh is raised at once. A crest survives only if it appears on every single one of them. Which crests are left?

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Loop from left to right and AND them all. Fine for three banners. But the range can run to two billion, and then we're looping until the next age.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then look at what a range of consecutive numbers does to the low bits. If the range holds more than one number, the lowest bit alternates between zero and one — so it is cleared, always.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The same argument climbs. Any bit that changes anywhere inside the range is guaranteed to be zero somewhere, and one zero is enough to wipe it out.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: So the only crests that survive are the ones the endpoints already agree on — the common leading prefix of left and right.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Five is one-oh-one and seven is one-one-one. They agree on the leading one, then disagree. So the answer is one followed by zeroes — four.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which gives an algorithm with no loop over the range at all: shift both endpoints right until they are equal, counting the shifts, then shift the agreed value back left by that count.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: At most thirty-two shifts, regardless of how wide the range is. Two billion banners, thirty-two steps.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is a second form worth knowing: repeatedly clear the lowest set bit of the right endpoint until it drops to or below the left one. Same reasoning, expressed with Kernighan's trick.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Iterating the range. Also, when left equals right, the answer is that number itself — the shift loop handles it, but only if it is written as "shift while they differ" rather than assuming at least one shift.

202.title: Happy Number
202.epTitle: The Fever That Either Breaks or Loops

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Repeatedly replace a number by the sum of the squares of its digits. It is happy if this eventually reaches 1; otherwise it loops forever. Determine whether a number is happy.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Kureha's fever chart: each reading becomes the sum of the squares of its digits. Some patients settle at one and recover. Some go round in circles forever.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So run it and see. But if it loops, 'run it and see' never finishes.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There are only two outcomes — reach one, or repeat a reading you have already had. Repeating means a cycle, and a cycle can never escape.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Nineteen gives eighty-two. Eighty-two gives sixty-eight. Sixty-eight gives one hundred. One hundred gives one. Recovered.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: A set of seen readings answers it. But look at the structure: each reading determines exactly one next reading. That is a linked list where the next pointer is a function.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Which means Floyd's tortoise and hare works — one reading advancing once per step, another advancing twice. If they ever meet, it's a loop.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And that costs no memory at all, where the set costs whatever the cycle's length is. Same answer, constant space.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Why does it always terminate? Couldn't the readings grow forever?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: No — a three-digit number can produce at most two hundred and forty-three, so everything is quickly trapped below a small ceiling. Finitely many values means it must either hit one or repeat.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Capping the iterations at an arbitrary number and hoping. The termination argument is that the values are bounded, so either 1 is reached or a value repeats — both are detectable exactly.

205.title: Isomorphic Strings
205.epTitle: The Cipher That Must Work Both Ways

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Two strings are isomorphic if the characters of the first can be replaced to get the second, preserving order, with no two characters mapping to the same character and each character mapping to itself consistently.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Dr. Kureha's notes are enciphered by swapping letters — but the swap has to be reversible. Each letter always becomes the same letter, and no two letters may collapse onto the same one.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So walk both strings together and record what each letter becomes. 'e' becomes 'a'. 'g' becomes 'd'. Then the second 'g' also becomes 'd' — consistent.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One map, then. What could go wrong?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Take 'badc' and 'baba'. Forward, 'b' becomes 'b', 'a' becomes 'a', 'd' becomes 'b'... and now two different letters both become 'b'. The forward map never noticed, because it only ever asked about the source.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So we need a second map going the other way, checking that nothing is claimed twice.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Two maps, checked at every position. If either disagrees with what it already recorded, the cipher is not reversible and the answer is no.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: There's a neater version, isn't there? Compare the pattern of first appearances.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Map each string to the sequence of positions where each character was first seen. 'egg' gives zero, one, one; 'add' gives zero, one, one. Identical, so they are isomorphic — one comparison instead of two maps.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Both are linear. The two-map version is easier to explain out loud, which matters more than it sounds.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Using only the forward map, which accepts "badc" and "baba". The failure requires two distinct source characters mapping onto one target, so simple test cases miss it entirely.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: There are numCourses courses labeled 0 to numCourses-1. Given a list of prerequisite pairs [a, b] meaning course b must be completed before course a, determine whether it's possible to finish all courses — that is, whether the prerequisite graph contains no cycle.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Four trials to earn passage past this island. The scroll says Trial 1 needs Trial 0 done first, Trial 2 also needs Trial 0, and Trial 3 needs BOTH Trial 1 and Trial 2 finished before you can attempt it. Can we even complete all four, or is there a loop trapping us?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Count how many un-cleared prerequisites each trial still has — its 'in-degree'. Trial 0 needs none. Trial 1 and Trial 2 each need one. Trial 3 needs two. Any trial with zero remaining prerequisites can be attempted right now.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Only Trial 0 starts at zero, so it goes in the queue first.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Clear Trial 0. Now anything that listed Trial 0 as a prerequisite gets to drop it — Trial 1's count goes from 1 to 0, Trial 2's count goes from 1 to 0. Both join the queue.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Clear Trial 1. Trial 3 needed it — drop Trial 3's count from 2 to 1. Not zero yet, so Trial 3 still waits.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Clear Trial 2. Trial 3 needed this one too — drop its count from 1 to 0. NOW Trial 3 joins the queue.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Clear Trial 3. Nothing left waiting on anything.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: We cleared all four trials — exactly numCourses of them. If even one trial had been stuck forever above zero, that would mean a cycle: two trials each secretly waiting on the other. But nothing got stuck here.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! No loop, no trap — just do them in this order: 0, then 1 and 2 in either order, then 3!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Peel off whatever's free right now, update what depended on it, repeat. If the queue ever runs dry before every trial is cleared, it's impossible.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Trying to detect the cycle with a single visited/unvisited flag during DFS instead of tracking the current recursion path (or, in the BFS version shown here, comparing the count of processed courses to numCourses) — a course can be fully explored down one branch and still sit on a cycle reachable from another branch.

208.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
208.epTitle: The Scroll That Branches by Letter

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Design a trie (prefix tree) that supports three operations: insert(word) adds a word; search(word) returns true only if that exact word was inserted; startsWith(prefix) returns true if any inserted word begins with that prefix.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Watch this, I'm building a scroll-tree! One node per letter, growing down from a single root — so any word that starts the same way shares the same trunk!

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: How do you even put a whole word like 'apple' into it?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Letter by letter. Starting at the root, for each letter I either follow an existing branch or grow a brand new one — then I step down onto it before reading the next letter.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: a-p-p-l-e: five new branches grow straight down from the root. The very last one gets marked as a true word ending, not just a passing letter.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: search('apple') just retraces that same path. Every letter exists, and the final node is flagged as a word ending — so it returns true.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Now try search('app'). The path a-p-p exists — we can walk it fine — but that second 'p' node was only ever a pass-through on the way to 'apple'. It was never flagged as an ending.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So search('app') returns false. Existing on the path is not enough — the node has to be specifically marked as somebody's actual word ending.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: But what if I just want to know if ANY word starts with 'app', I don't care if 'app' itself is a whole word?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is startsWith — same walk, but we skip the end-flag check entirely. The path a-p-p exists, so startsWith('app') returns true, even though search('app') just told us false.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Now insert('app')! No new branches needed at all — that second 'p' node already exists, we just raise its ending flag.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: search('app') returns true now. Same tree, one flag flipped.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is a trie in full: shared trunks for shared prefixes, and a single flag per node deciding whether that exact point is a real word.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Implementing search() by only checking whether the final node exists, without checking its end-of-word flag, silently makes search() behave identically to startsWith() — which is exactly why search('app') must return false even though the 'app' path is fully present.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of positive integers and a target, return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least the target. Return 0 if no such subarray exists.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The Baroque Works agents will only fall asleep once the crew has drunk at least seven barrels — and Zoro wants it done in as FEW consecutive rounds as possible. He can't skip a round in the middle; whatever he starts, he finishes.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So try every starting round and count forward from each? Six starts, six counts each — fine here, awful on a real night.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Watch what the barrels have in common: every one of them is positive. So adding a round can only raise the total, and dropping a round from the front can only lower it. That is a licence to slide a window instead of restarting.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Grow from the right while we're short. Two, then five, then six — still under seven. Then the fourth round brings it to eight. We've cleared the bar for the first time, with four rounds.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Now shrink from the left, as long as we still clear it. Drop the first two: six. That's short — so four rounds was as tight as that window goes. Put the barrel back conceptually and move on.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Add the fifth round, four barrels — that's ten. Now shrink hard: drop the 3, leaves seven. Still enough. Drop the 1, leaves six — too few, so stop. Three rounds that time.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Add the last round, three barrels — ten again. Shrink: drop the 1 and the 2 and we're at seven with just two rounds standing. Drop another and we fall short.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Two rounds. And notice neither edge ever went backwards — the right edge walked the line once and the left edge walked it once. Two pointers, 2n moves total, no matter how the nesting looks in the code.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And if the whole night doesn't add up to seven at all? Then we never once cleared the bar, and the answer has to be zero — not some leftover window length.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is why 'best' starts at infinity and is translated to zero at the end if it was never touched. And one warning: put a single negative barrel on that table and the whole licence collapses — shrinking would no longer be guaranteed to lower the sum.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Returning the last window length instead of 0 when the target is never reached. And the deeper trap: this technique needs all values positive. With negatives, shrinking can raise the sum, so you must use prefix sums with a map instead.

210.title: Course Schedule II
210.epTitle: The Order the Training Must Be Done

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given numCourses and a list of prerequisite pairs, return an ordering of courses you can take to finish them all. Return an empty array if no such ordering exists.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Rayleigh's training has an order to it. Some drills can't start until others are finished. Give me a sequence that works — or tell me there isn't one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Each drill is a node; each prerequisite is a directed edge pointing from what must come first to what it unlocks. What you want is a topological order.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So start with whatever has no prerequisites at all.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Count, for each drill, how many prerequisites it is waiting on — its in-degree. Everything sitting at zero can be started immediately, so put all of those in a queue.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Drill zero has nothing before it. Take it. That releases one and two — each of them was waiting only on zero, so both drop to zero.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Take one: drill three drops from two prerequisites to one — not ready. Take two: three drops to zero and joins the queue.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Then three. Four drills, in an order that never breaks a prerequisite.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And if the training were circular — three needs one, one needs three?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then neither ever reaches in-degree zero, the queue empties early, and we finish having emitted fewer drills than exist. That count is the cycle test: emit fewer than n and there is no valid order at all.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: So the check isn't a separate pass. It falls out of the same run.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is a depth-first form too — post-order, reversed — which detects the cycle by finding an edge back into a node still on the current stack. Kahn's version is easier to explain out loud, and being able to explain it is most of the interview.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Reading the pair the wrong way round. In [a, b] here, b must come before a, so the edge points b → a. Reversing it produces a plausible-looking order that is exactly backwards.

211.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Design a data structure that supports adding words and then searching for a word, where the search word may contain "." characters that can match any single letter. addWord(word) adds a word; search(word) returns true if some added word matches, treating "." as a wildcard for one letter.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: Yohoho~ Three wanted posters go up on the same board tonight: bad, dad, mad. All rhyme, all three letters, all end the same way!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Same trie idea as always — each word gets its own branch from the root, and the very last letter of each gets flagged as a true ending.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Someone asks for 'pad'. With three posters up that is nothing, but imagine thousands — we do not want to compare 'pad' letter-by-letter against every single stored word by hand.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: We do not have to. At the root we look for a branch labeled 'p' — there is none. Dead end immediately, no letters left to check.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: search('bad') is the easy case. Walk b, a, d — every letter matches a real branch, and the last one is flagged. True.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: Now the weird one — '.ad'. That dot could be ANYTHING! How do you follow a branch that isn't even a real letter?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: You do not follow one branch — you try all of them. At a '.', branch out into every child the current node has, and keep searching down each one. If even ONE of those paths finishes as a match, the whole search is true.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: '.ad': at the root the dot tries b, d, and m all at once. Following 'b' first: then 'a' matches for real, then 'd' matches and it is flagged. Found a match — stop right there.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And 'b..'? First letter is fixed as 'b', no wildcard there. But the next two are both dots — so from the 'b' branch, try every child at each level.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: From 'b', the only child is 'a' — the first dot matches it. From there, the only child is the flagged 'd' — the second dot matches that too. True.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Every dot just means: branch into all children here instead of one.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Treating '.' as matching zero-or-more letters (like a regex star) instead of exactly one letter is a common mix-up — here every '.' must consume precisely one position in the word, so the DFS still needs to track remaining length exactly, it just fans out over children when it hits a dot.

212.title: Word Search II
212.epTitle: Every Name on the Execution Roll

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an m x n grid of letters and a list of words, return every word that can be spelled by walking through adjacent cells (up, down, left, right) without reusing a cell within one word.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The execution roll is a grid of letters, and Marine headquarters has a list of names it wants found in it. A name is spelled by walking cell to cell — up, down, left, right — never standing on the same cell twice within one name.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Easy. Take the first name, search the whole grid for it. Then the second name, search the whole grid again. Then the third...

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: There are three thousand names on that roll. You'd walk the same grid three thousand times, and every walk starts by exploring the same dead ends.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So carry all the names at once. Stack them into a prefix tree — every name that starts with the same letters shares the same branch, right up to the point where they diverge.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Now one walk of the grid carries every name simultaneously. From each cell I step to a neighbour and ask the tree a single question: is anything still spelled this way?

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: And the instant the answer is no, I stop. Not one name abandoned — every name that begins with those letters, all at once. That's the cut.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Walking from the top-left 'o': o-a is still alive, o-a-t is still alive, o-a-t-h — and this node is marked as the end of a name. Found one.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: But 'p' isn't anywhere in the grid at all, so 'pea' dies on the very first letter. We never walk a single step for it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One more discipline. When we step onto a cell we must mark it used, and when we step back off it we must UNMARK it — otherwise a cell consumed by one path stays blocked for every other path forever.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Choose, walk, un-choose. Same as any search that has to try more than one road out of the same crossroads.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: One last thing — 'eat' is spelled twice in that grid. We shouldn't hand headquarters the same name twice.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So when a name is found, we clear its end-marker in the tree. It can never be reported again — and as a bonus, branches that no longer lead anywhere can be pruned away entirely, which makes the rest of the search faster still.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting to un-mark a visited cell on the way back out, which silently blocks every other path through it. Second: reporting a word every time it is spelled — clear the end-marker on the trie node once found, so duplicates are impossible.

215.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an unsorted array of numbers and an integer k, find the k-th LARGEST value in the array (not the k-th distinct value — duplicates count by position).

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Weatheria's tracking six storm readings: 3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4. We need the SECOND-strongest one, k = 2.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Sort all six and grab index 1 — that works, but it's O(n log n) and we'd re-sort readings we don't even care about.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Instead, keep a min-heap that holds only the k STRONGEST readings seen so far. Every time it grows past size k, evict the weakest one inside it. Whatever survives on top at the end is exactly the k-th largest.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Reading 3: heap has room, just drop it in.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Reading 2: heap has room (size 2 = k), drop it in too. Weakest on top is 2.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Reading 1: push it in, now size 3 — over capacity. Evict the weakest, which is 1 itself.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Reading 5: push, size 3, evict weakest — that's 2 this time.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Reading 6: push, size 3, evict weakest — 3 goes.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Reading 4: push, size 3, evict weakest — 4 is the smallest of the three, so it's the one that leaves immediately.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: No readings left. The weakest survivor still sitting on top of our size-2 heap is 5 — that's the 2nd-strongest storm.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! We only ever kept two readings around at once, no matter how many storms rolled in!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: That's the point — the heap never holds more than k.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Building a max-heap out of ALL n elements (or fully sorting the array) instead of capping a min-heap at size k. It still gives the right answer, but costs O(n log n) time and O(n) space instead of O(n log k) and O(k) — wasteful when k is much smaller than n.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array and an integer k, return true if there are two distinct indices i and j such that the values are equal and the indices differ by at most k.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The same symptom twice is normal. The same symptom twice within three days is a relapse — and that we need to catch.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Compare every pair of days and check both the value and the gap? That's every pair again.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Two ways to do it in one pass. Either remember the last day each symptom appeared, and check the gap when it reappears — or keep a window of the last k days as a set.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The window version is neat. Slide forward, and whenever the window grows past k days, drop the oldest one out of the set.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then a duplicate INSIDE the set is automatically within k days — the distance check is built into what the set contains, rather than being a separate comparison.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Day zero: symptom one, window holds one. Day one: two. Day two: three. With k of three the window still holds all of them, so day three's one is already there. Relapse.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And with k of two, day zero would have been dropped by then, so the same data gives no relapse.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The last-seen map does the same job and generalises better — replacing the position each time means you always compare against the NEAREST previous occurrence, which is the only one that can be close enough.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Keeping the nearest rather than the first. That's the detail I'd have got wrong.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Storing the FIRST index a value was seen at rather than the most recent. Only the nearest previous occurrence can satisfy the distance bound, so the map entry must be overwritten every time.

221.title: Maximal Square
221.epTitle: The Largest Square of Solid Stone

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a binary matrix, find the largest square containing only 1s and return its area.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Which is the biggest solid square of intact floor in the chamber? Not a rectangle — a square, all ones, no gaps.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Try every square at every position and check it? That's an enormous amount of re-checking the same stone.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Anchor the state instead. Let each cell hold the side of the largest solid square whose BOTTOM-RIGHT corner is that cell. Then every cell is answered once.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And how big can that square be?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One more than the smallest of the three squares ending above, to the left, and diagonally back. All three must support it — the weakest of them is the binding constraint.

clips.speaker: chopper
