clips.line: So if any one of those three is small, this corner can't extend past it, no matter how solid the other two are.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And a cell holding a zero has a square of side zero — no branching needed, the recurrence simply never fires there.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Then the answer is the largest side anywhere, squared. It's the AREA they asked for, not the side.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Anchoring a shape at one of its corners is the reusable idea here — it turns 'find the biggest' into 'answer this cell', which is what makes it a DP at all.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Returning the side length instead of the area. Taking the maximum of the three neighbours rather than the minimum — that computes something that is not a square at all.

222.title: Count Complete Tree Nodes
222.epTitle: Counting the Rivets Without Counting Them

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the root of a complete binary tree, count its nodes in better than O(n) time.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Count the rivets in the frame. Walking every one is easy — but the frame is COMPLETE, filled left to right with no gaps except possibly at the end of the last row. That must be worth something.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: It is worth a great deal. A PERFECT tree of height h holds exactly two to the h, minus one, nodes — no traversal needed at all.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So how do we tell whether a subtree is perfect?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Walk its leftmost spine and its rightmost spine. In a complete tree, if those two heights are equal the subtree is perfect — and the formula answers it instantly.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And if they differ, recurse into both children — but at most one of those will need real work, because the other is guaranteed perfect.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is what gives the bound: log n levels, each costing a log n spine walk. O of log squared n instead of O of n.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: It's marked Easy, which feels like a joke. The O of n traversal is easy; using the completeness is not.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And that is the lesson. When a problem states a structural guarantee, it is there to be used — otherwise why mention it?

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Ignoring completeness and just counting every node, which is correct but misses the entire point. And computing the two heights by full traversal rather than by walking the spines.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Evaluate a string expression containing non-negative integers, +, -, brackets and spaces, without using any built-in expression evaluator.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Cricket's debts are written in nested brackets, with plus and minus only — but a minus in front of a bracket flips everything inside it.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So we need to remember, when we go into a bracket, what was outside it. That's a stack again — but of what, exactly?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Of two things: the total accumulated so far, and the sign that applies to the bracket we are about to enter. Push both, then start fresh inside.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And on the closing bracket, the inner total is finished — multiply it by the saved sign and add it back to the saved total.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Everything else is a single left-to-right sweep. A digit extends the number being read. A plus sets the sign to one, a minus to minus one. A number, once complete, is added with that sign.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Numbers can be more than one digit, so I have to keep building until the digits stop rather than reading one character as one number.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And the last number has no operator after it, so it must be added once the sweep ends — the same 'flush what is left' step as every other one-pass parser.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: There's no multiplication here at all, which is why a sign and a running total are enough. Precedence would change everything.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: With multiplication and division you would need to hold the previous operand back so it can be combined before adding — that is Basic Calculator II, and it is a genuinely different shape.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Reading multi-digit numbers one character at a time. And forgetting to add the final number after the loop, since nothing follows it to trigger the add.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the root of a binary tree, invert it — swap every node's left and right subtrees — and return the root.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Dock One's layout has to be rebuilt as a mirror image — every berth that was on the left goes to the right, all the way down.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is one of the shortest recursions there is. Swap this node's two children, then invert each of them. Or invert them first and then swap — both orders work.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Four's children swap: seven comes left, two goes right. Then two's own children swap, and seven's.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Why do both orders work? Surely one of them mangles it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Because the swap only touches this node's two pointers, and the recursion only touches what is below them. The two operations are independent, so their order is free.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The null case is the whole base case — an absent node inverts to an absent node.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And if the recursion depth worries you, the iterative version is the same thing with a queue or a stack: take a node, swap its children, push both.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: It's famous, this one. Someone was turned down for a job over it.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Recursing into node.left after already overwriting it, so one subtree is inverted twice and the other not at all — swap using a simultaneous assignment or a temporary.

228.title: Summary Ranges
228.epTitle: The Roll Call of the Rebel Army

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a sorted array of distinct integers, return the smallest sorted list of ranges that covers every number exactly once. A range of one number is written on its own; a longer run is written as "start->end".

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Vivi needs the rebel roll call summarised before dawn. We have every surviving squad number, already in order, no repeats — but reading out six thousand numbers one at a time will take all night.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So we shout the blocks instead! 'Squads zero through two, present!' Anything that runs unbroken gets one call.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then the only thing we ever need to notice is where a run BREAKS. Since the numbers are sorted and distinct, a run continues exactly when the next number is one more than this one.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Zero. One is next, so that's still the same block. Two is next — still the same block. Then four. Four is not three, so the block ends here.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Call it: squads zero through two. Then a new block opens at four. Five follows it, so the block grows. Seven does not follow five, so we close it.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And then seven is alone at the end. There's nothing after it at all — so the run of length one just gets shouted as itself. Not 'seven through seven'. That would sound ridiculous.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Notice the shape of it. We remember only where the current block STARTED, and we walk forward closing it the moment the chain snaps. One pass, and nothing is stored twice.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Three calls instead of six. And on the real roll — six thousand numbers — that's a handful of shouts instead of a night of them.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The last block is the one that gets people. There's no 'next number' to break it, so if you only close blocks on a break, the final one never gets called at all!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is why the loop closes the block when the chain snaps, and once more when the line ends. Two places, same closing move.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting to emit the final block. There is no "next" element to break the last run, so the close has to happen both on a break and after the loop. The other classic is printing 7->7 for a single number instead of just 7.

230.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the root of a binary search tree (BST) and an integer k, find the k-th smallest value stored in the tree (k is 1-indexed, so k=1 means the smallest).

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Sengoku's vault is sorted like a search tree: k = 3. We need the 3rd-smallest bounty on file — without dumping every entry out and sorting them again.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Here's the trick: an INORDER walk — all of the left branch, then the node itself, then all of the right branch — visits every BST node in strictly ascending order automatically. That's just what left-smaller/right-bigger means, applied recursively.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So instead of pulling all six values into a list and sorting — O(n log n) — we walk in that order and just COUNT, stopping the instant we hit the k-th one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Dive left first, as far as it goes: 5 to 3.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Still left: 3 to 2.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Still left: 2 to 1 — no left child left. This is the smallest value in the whole tree, so the walk finally visits it first.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Visit 1: count = 1. Not k yet. 1 has no right child either, so step back up to 2.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Visit 2: count = 2. Still not k. No right child under 2 either, so step back up to 3.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Visit 3: count = 3. That's k! The 3rd smallest value is 3 — stop right here.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! And we never even had to look at 4, 5, or 6!

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: That early stop matters a lot when k is small but the vault has thousands of entries — no reason to sort the whole thing.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Doing a full inorder traversal into a list first and then indexing list[k-1]. That always costs O(n) time and O(n) space, even when k is 1 — stopping the walk the moment the count hits k avoids visiting the rest of the tree at all.

236.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
236.epTitle: Where the Two Routes Last Met

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a binary tree and two nodes, find their lowest common ancestor — the deepest node having both as descendants, where a node may be a descendant of itself.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Two crews set out from the same yard and took different routes. Where did their paths last coincide?

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Record the full route to each and compare them? That works, but it needs both routes stored.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There is a recursion that needs nothing. Ask each node one question: did you find either target anywhere below you, or are you one of them?

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: If a node IS one of the targets, it reports itself and stops looking — because a node counts as its own descendant.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Otherwise it asks both children. If BOTH report a find, the two routes diverge exactly here — so this node is the answer.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And if only one side reports, the answer lies that way, so we pass the finding straight up unchanged.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The subtlety is that the same return value carries two meanings — 'here is a target I found' on the way up, and 'here is the answer' once both sides have reported. It works because once both report, that value can only ever be passed upward unchanged.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And this assumes both targets are actually in the tree. If one might be missing, you'd need to confirm the find rather than trusting it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which the problem guarantees. In a BST you can do better still — compare both values against the node and simply walk down, in O of height with no recursion at all.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Assuming both nodes exist — if one may be absent, the algorithm returns the other one, which is wrong. Also, a node is its own descendant, so a target that is an ancestor of the other IS the answer.

238.title: Product of Array Except Self
238.epTitle: The Gate of Justice Dial Lock

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of integers, return an array where each element is the product of all the OTHER elements — without using division, in O(n) time.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The Gate of Justice control panel — four dials. CP9 designed it so no single dial's correct setting can be read off directly: each dial's true value has to equal the PRODUCT of all three OTHER dials.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: So multiply the other three together for each dial. What's the problem?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One dial currently reads zero. The lazy shortcut — multiply ALL four dials, then divide by each one — breaks the instant you divide by that zero. We need a way that never divides at all.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: First sweep, left to right: a running product of everything BEFORE each dial. Nothing sits before dial one — its 'before' product is 1. Carry dial one's own value, 4, forward for whoever's next.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Dial two: everything before it is just dial one — 'before' product 4. Dial three: everything before it is dial one and two — 4 times 3 is 12.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Dial four: everything before it includes the zero dial — so its 'before' product is 0. That's not a mistake to fix — dial three genuinely erases everything that comes after it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Second sweep, right to left: a running product of everything AFTER each dial, combined with what we already have. Dial four: nothing after it — combine with 1. Its answer stays 0.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Dial three: everything after it is just dial four, value 5. Combine: 12 times 5 is 60. Dial three's true setting is 60.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Dial two: everything after it includes dial three's zero — 4 times 0 is 0. Dial one: everything after it also includes that same zero — 1 times 0 is 0.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Final dial: 0 too, for the same reason. Three of the four true settings are zero, and only dial three actually matters — and we never divided by the zero dial that would have crashed the whole calculation.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Two clean sweeps. Left to right, then right to left. No division anywhere. Let's move.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Computing the total product of the whole array and dividing by nums[i] for each answer — this crashes outright when any element is zero, and silently produces all-zero output when two or more elements are zero, instead of the correct single non-zero answer.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given two strings, determine whether the second is an anagram of the first — the same letters with the same multiplicities, in any order.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Two labels from the medicine cabinet. Same letters, shuffled — or genuinely different compounds? Getting this wrong would be unfortunate.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Sort both and compare. Two lines, done.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Correct, and perfectly acceptable — n log n. But counting does it in linear time, and the counting version generalises to the harder problems in this family.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: One tally. Add one for every letter of the first label, subtract one for every letter of the second.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: If they are anagrams, every entry ends at zero. A single non-zero entry anywhere means the labels differ.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And different lengths can be rejected immediately, before any counting at all.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One tally rather than two, and one pass over each string. For lowercase English, that tally is a fixed array of twenty-six — genuinely constant space.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And if the labels were in Japanese? Then twenty-six is nowhere near enough.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then a hash map instead of an array, and the space becomes proportional to the distinct characters present. The follow-up in this problem asks exactly that, and it is a real consideration rather than a formality.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting the length check, which is both a free rejection and necessary if you only verify that no count goes negative. Also, order is irrelevant here — this is the exact opposite of the subsequence question.

274.title: H-Index
274.epTitle: The Bounty That Proves a Reputation

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of citation counts, return the h-index: the largest h such that at least h papers have h or more citations each.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: A pirate's standing is measured like this: the largest number h such that at least h of their bounties are worth h million or more.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: That definition ties itself in a knot. The answer appears on both sides of it.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So sort the bounties from largest down. Then walk them and ask: is the bounty in position i worth at least i plus one?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Six is at least one. Five is at least two. Three is at least three. But one is not at least four. So the answer is three.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Sorting makes the self-reference collapse, because position and count line up.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: That's n log n, though. Can we do better?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Yes — counting sort. The h-index can never exceed the number of papers, so every bounty above that ceiling can be lumped into one bucket. Count how many fall in each bucket, then sweep downward accumulating.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Because a value larger than the paper count can't raise h any further. The ceiling is what makes bucketing possible.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Comparing the value at position i against i rather than i+1 when using zero-based indexing. And forgetting that citations above n can all be lumped into a single bucket, which is what makes the linear version work.

289.title: Game of Life
289.epTitle: The Island That Changes All at Once

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an m x n board of live (1) and dead (0) cells, compute the next state, where every cell updates simultaneously according to its eight neighbours. Solve it in place.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Little Garden's undergrowth advances by its own rules, and every patch changes at the same instant — not one after another. Two or three neighbours and you live; exactly three and a bare patch sprouts.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So I walk the board and update each patch. ...No, wait. If I update the first patch, the second patch counts its neighbours against a board that's already changed.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is the whole difficulty. 'Simultaneous' means every cell must read the OLD board while the NEW one is being written. Copying the board solves it instantly and costs O(m·n) space.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And the follow-up asks for in place. So each cell has to hold both answers at once.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Use two bits. The low bit stays the current state, untouched, so every neighbour count still reads the old board. The second bit records what the cell becomes.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So a cell that is alive now and alive next holds three. Alive now, dead next holds one. Dead now, alive next holds two.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And counting neighbours means reading their low bit only — masking with one. Then a second pass shifts every cell right by one, and the next state becomes the current one.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Two passes, no copy, and the simultaneity is preserved exactly.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: What about the edges? A patch on the border has fewer than eight neighbours.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Bounds-check each of the eight offsets and simply skip the ones off the board — an absent neighbour is not a dead neighbour, it is no neighbour. Keeping the eight directions in a list rather than writing them out is what keeps that loop readable.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Updating cells one at a time against a mutating board, which makes the result depend on scan order. Also, after encoding, neighbour counts must mask the low bit — reading the raw value counts cells that have merely been marked.

290.title: Word Pattern
290.epTitle: The Signal Flags and What They Stand For

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a pattern of letters and a sentence of words, determine whether the sentence follows the pattern — a full bijection between letters and words.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The signal flags spell out a pattern, and the shouted message is supposed to follow it. Same flag, same word. Different flags, different words.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: This is the letter cipher again, with words on one side instead of characters. Split the sentence, then walk the flags and the words in step.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: 'a' means dog. 'b' means cat. The second 'b' must mean cat — it does. The last 'a' must mean dog — it does.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And the trap is the same one — 'abba' against four dogs. Forward, 'a' means dog and 'b' means dog, no contradiction at all.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So the reverse map matters just as much: once 'dog' is claimed by 'a', no other flag may claim it. Two maps, both checked.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: There's a check before any of that, though. If there are four flags and only three words, nothing can possibly line up.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And it is easy to miss, because zipping two sequences of different lengths in most languages simply stops at the shorter one — silently accepting a mismatch instead of rejecting it.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So the length check isn't defensive tidying. It's a real case the rest of the code cannot see.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Zipping pattern and words without first comparing their lengths, so "abc" against "dog cat" is accepted. Also, splitting on a single space assumes no repeated or trailing spaces.

295.title: Find Median from Data Stream
295.epTitle: The Scales That Never Stop Tipping

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Design a structure that accepts numbers one at a time and can report the median of everything seen so far, at any moment.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The tally of every deal at the tea party keeps growing, and Big Mom wants the MIDDLE value on demand — not at the end, at any moment.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Keep a sorted list and insert each new number in its place? Finding the spot is a binary search, so that's fast...

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Finding it is fast. Making room for it is not — everything after the insertion point shifts along. That is linear work on every single deal.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: But look at what the median actually needs. Not the whole ordering — only the boundary between the smaller half and the larger half. So hold the halves separately.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: A max-heap for the low half, so its top is the LARGEST of the small ones. A min-heap for the high half, so its top is the SMALLEST of the large ones. The median sits right between those two tops.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Add one. It goes to the low half. One heap holds one item, the other none — so the median is just that top: one.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Add two. It belongs on the high side. Now both halves hold one, so the median is the average of the two tops: one and a half.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Add three. High side again — but now it holds two and the low side holds one. Rebalance: move the high side's smallest across. Median is two.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The rebalance is the whole discipline. The two halves must never differ in size by more than one, or the tops stop straddling the middle and the answer quietly drifts.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: There's a neat trick for the insert, isn't there? Push onto one heap, immediately move its top to the other, and then fix the sizes.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Yes — it routes the value to the correct half without a single comparison against the tops. Insert costs log n, and reading the median costs nothing at all: it is one or two peeks.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Letting the halves drift out of balance by more than one element — the tops then no longer straddle the middle. And in a language with only a min-heap, remember to negate on the low side, including when reading its top back.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an array of numbers, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence — the elements must appear in order but need not be adjacent.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The satellites pass overhead in a fixed order, and we can only lock onto ones that are higher than the last one we locked. Skipping is allowed — but going back in time is not. How long a chain can we get?

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: For every satellite, look at all the earlier ones lower than it and take the best chain ending there, plus one. That works! It's just... every pair. Slow.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: It works, and it is the honest starting point — order n squared. But there is a sharper structure hiding here. Instead of the chains themselves, track the SMALLEST possible ending value for a chain of each length.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Ten arrives. The best chain of length one now ends at ten. Nine arrives — a chain of length one that ends at nine is strictly better than one ending at ten, because nine leaves more room above it.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Wait — we just threw away ten. But it might have been part of the answer!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Only its VALUE was replaced, never its length. Any chain that could have been built on ten can also be built on nine, and possibly more. We are keeping the length record and lowering the bar.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Two arrives — lower still, so length one now ends at two. Then five: five is higher than two, so it EXTENDS. Length two now ends at five.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Three arrives. It can't extend past five, but a length-two chain ending at three is better than one ending at five. So it replaces five.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Seven extends to length three. A hundred and one extends to length four. Eighteen cannot extend past a hundred and one, but it lowers the length-four bar to eighteen.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Four entries in the table, so the longest chain is four. And because that table is always sorted, finding where a new value belongs is a binary search — which drops the whole thing to n log n.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So the table is the answer chain, right? Two, three, seven, eighteen — that IS a valid chain here.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Coincidence. The table is a record of best endings per length, not a real subsequence — its entries can come from positions in the wrong order. Only its LENGTH is meaningful. To recover an actual chain you must track predecessors separately.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Believing the tails array is the answer subsequence — it is not, and its contents may never have co-existed. Also, "strictly increasing" means the binary search must find the first tail ≥ x; using > silently solves the non-decreasing variant instead.

322.title: Coin Change
322.epTitle: The Fewest Coins to Buy the Log Pose

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a set of coin denominations and a target amount, return the fewest number of coins needed to make that amount exactly, using an unlimited supply of each denomination. If it's impossible to make that exact amount, return -1.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: We owe exactly 6 Berries for the Log Pose, and our coin pouch only has denominations of 1, 3, and 4. We can use as many of each as we like — what's the FEWEST coins that add up to exactly 6?

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Trying every combination of coins sounds like it could take forever if the amount's big!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So build it up instead. For every amount from 0 to 6, ask: for each coin no bigger than this amount, what's 1 plus the fewest coins needed for (amount minus that coin)? Take the smallest result. Amount 0 needs 0 coins — that's free.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Amount 1: only coin 1 fits. 1 + ways(0) = 1 + 0 = 1 coin.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Amount 2: only coin 1 fits (twice, effectively). 1 + ways(1) = 1 + 1 = 2 coins.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Amount 3: coin 1 gives 1 + ways(2) = 3. But coin 3 gives 1 + ways(0) = 1. The smaller wins — just 1 coin.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Amount 4: coin 1 gives 1 + ways(3) = 2. Coin 3 gives 1 + ways(1) = 2. Coin 4 gives 1 + ways(0) = 1. Smallest is 1 coin.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Amount 5: coin 1 gives 1 + ways(4) = 2. Coin 3 gives 1 + ways(2) = 3. Coin 4 gives 1 + ways(1) = 2. Smallest is 2 coins.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Amount 6, the target: coin 1 gives 1 + ways(5) = 3. Coin 3 gives 1 + ways(3) = 2. Coin 4 gives 1 + ways(2) = 3. Smallest is 2 coins — that's coin 3 twice.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Two coins, both threes, and we're set sail!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Every amount only ever needs the answers already sitting below it. Nothing gets recomputed twice.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Initializing unreachable amounts to 0 instead of infinity (or amount+1) — that makes an impossible amount look like it costs 0 coins, silently poisoning every larger amount that builds on it. Any table entry still at infinity at the end means -1, not 0.

373.title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
373.epTitle: The Smallest Slices of Two Cakes

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given two sorted arrays and an integer k, return the k pairs (one element from each array) with the smallest sums.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Two cakes, each already cut and laid out smallest slice first. We need the three cheapest combinations — one slice from each.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Make every combination, sort them, take three. Nine pairs here — but with a thousand slices each that's a million pairs to build and sort, for three answers.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: We only need three, so we should only ever build a handful. Picture the pairs as a grid: rows from the first cake, columns from the second. Both cakes are sorted, so sums increase as you go right and as you go down.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So the very smallest pair is the top-left corner. One and two — three Berries.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And the next smallest must be adjacent to something already taken — either one step right, or one step down. So keep a heap of the frontier: the cheapest untaken pairs on the border of what we've claimed.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Start with the whole first column in the heap: one-and-two, seven-and-two, eleven-and-two. Pop the smallest — one and two. Then push only its right-hand neighbour, one and four.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Pop again: one and four beats seven and two, five against nine. Push one and six. Pop again: one and six, seven Berries, still beats nine.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Three pops, and the heap never held more than a few entries. We never built the other six pairs at all.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Why push only the right-hand neighbour and not the one below as well?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Because the entire first column went in at the start, so every downward move is already accounted for. Push both and the same pair arrives twice — the classic duplicate bug in this pattern. Seed a column, then only ever walk right.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Pushing both the right and the down neighbour after each pop, which enqueues the same pair by two different routes. Seed a column and advance only along rows — or keep a visited set, which costs more.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Design a structure supporting insert, remove and getRandom, all in average O(1) time, where getRandom returns a uniformly random element currently present.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The lottery barrel has to do three things instantly: take a token, remove a named token, and draw a fair random one.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: A hash set does the first two. But drawing uniformly from a set means walking it — that's linear.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: A fair draw needs contiguous indexing, so an array is forced. And removing a named token needs a lookup, so a map is forced. Keep both.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: But removing from the middle of an array shifts everything after it.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So do not remove from the middle. Swap the doomed token with the LAST one, then pop the end. The array stays dense and nothing shifts.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And the map entry for the token that moved has to be updated, or the next lookup points at the wrong slot.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That single line is what people forget. Then a draw is one random index into a dense array — genuinely uniform, genuinely constant.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Two structures, each covering what the other cannot do. Same shape as the cache design.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting to update the map entry of the element moved into the vacated slot. And removing from the middle of the array, which is O(n) and destroys the whole design.

383.title: Ransom Note
383.epTitle: The Letter Cut From the Newspaper

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given two strings, return true if the first can be constructed using the letters of the second, where each letter of the second may be used at most once.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Wapol's demand note was cut from the castle newspaper. If we can prove every letter in the note came from that one issue, we know where it was written.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So check every letter of the note appears in the paper. Put the paper's letters in a set and look each one up.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That answers the wrong question. A set records that a letter exists, not how many there were. A note needing two 'a's would pass on a paper holding only one — you cannot cut the same letter out twice.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So counts, not membership. Tally every letter in the paper, then walk the note spending them.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: First 'a' of the note: the tally drops to one. Second 'a': the tally drops to zero. Nothing ever goes negative, so the note fits.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And the moment a tally would go below zero, we stop and say no. We don't even need to read the rest of the note.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One pass to build the tally, one pass to spend it. Linear in both lengths, and the tally is at most twenty-six entries, so the space is effectively constant.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The distinction between a set and a count map is the whole problem, isn't it. Everything else is bookkeeping.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Using a set and losing multiplicity. Also, an early exit is possible the moment the note is longer than the magazine — a free O(1) rejection worth mentioning.

392.title: Is Subsequence
392.epTitle: The Message Hidden in the Log

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given strings s and t, decide whether s is a subsequence of t — that is, whether s can be formed by deleting some characters of t without reordering the rest.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: A message has been hidden inside the ship's log. The letters of the message appear in the log in order — but with other letters scattered between them. Nothing is rearranged; only padded.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So we check every way of picking three letters out of the log? That's an enormous number of combinations for a log this size.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: No need to choose. Read the log straight through with a finger on the message. Every time the log gives me the letter my finger is on, the finger advances. Otherwise I just keep reading.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Log starts with 'a'. My finger is on 'a'. Match — finger moves to 'b'.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Log gives 'h'. Not 'b'. Keep reading. Log gives 'b' — match, finger moves to 'c'. Then 'g', then 'd', neither of them 'c', keep reading. Then 'c'. Match.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The finger ran off the end of the message, which is precisely what success looks like — every letter was found, in order.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: But hold on. When the log offered that first 'a', what if there was a better 'a' further along? Shouldn't we consider waiting?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Never. Taking the earliest match leaves the longest possible remainder of the log for everything still to be matched. Waiting can only shorten what is left. Greedy is not a gamble here — it is provably safe.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: One pass of the log, one finger, no memory of what came before. If the log ends and the finger hasn't cleared the message, the message isn't in there.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And if there are a thousand different messages to check against the SAME log? Reading the whole log a thousand times seems wasteful...

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then you pre-index the log once: for every letter, the sorted list of positions where it appears. After that each message is answered with a binary search per character, and the log is never re-read.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Confusing subsequence with substring or with anagram. A subsequence allows gaps but forbids reordering; comparing character counts answers "anagram" and would wrongly accept s = "cba".

399.title: Evaluate Division
399.epTitle: The Exchange Rates of the Human Shop

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given equations like a / b = 2.0 and a list of queries, return the value of each query, or -1.0 if it cannot be determined from the given equations.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: The Human Shop quotes rates in pairs. One 'a' buys two 'b'. One 'b' buys three 'c'. Nobody will tell us what an 'a' buys in 'c' — but it is obviously six.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So it's a chain. Follow the rates and multiply along the way.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which makes it a graph: each currency is a node, each quoted rate is an edge weighted by that rate — and the reverse edge exists too, weighted by one over it, because a rate always works both ways.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So a query is a path, and its answer is the product of the weights along that path.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Any path will do — the rates are consistent by assumption, so a longer route gives the same product. Depth-first search with a visited set is enough; nothing here needs shortest paths.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And 'e'? Nobody ever quoted anything against 'e'.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then it sits in its own component and the answer is minus one. Same for any currency that was never mentioned at all — asking about an unknown node is not zero, it is undetermined.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: There's one lovely special case. What is 'a' over 'a'?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One — but only if 'a' appears somewhere in the equations. If we have never heard of it, we cannot even assert that, and the answer is minus one. That distinction is the single most missed case in this problem.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And with thousands of queries against the same rate table?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then union-find with weights, or precompute every pair once. But for the sizes in this problem, a DFS per query is clean and fast enough — and clean beats clever when the constraints allow it.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Returning 1.0 for x/x when x was never mentioned in any equation — it must be -1.0. Also, forgetting to add the reciprocal edge, which leaves half the graph unreachable.

427.title: Construct Quad Tree
427.epTitle: The Four Quarters of the Frozen Half

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given an n x n grid of 0s and 1s where n is a power of two, build a quad tree: a node is a leaf if its region is uniform, otherwise it splits into four children covering the four quadrants.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Punk Hazard has to be charted, and half of it is burning while half is frozen. Storing every square metre separately would be absurd — most of the island is uniform for miles.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: So we record big uniform regions as single entries, and only split where the terrain actually changes?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is a quad tree. Ask one question of a square region: is it all the same? If yes, it is a leaf and we are finished with it. If no, cut it into four quarters and ask each of them the same question.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: The whole island isn't uniform — it's fire and ice. So the root splits.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: North-west quarter: all frozen. Leaf, value zero. North-east: all burning. Leaf, value one.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: South-west: burning. South-east: frozen. Four leaves, and the root that holds them.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The recursion is the same shape as every divide and conquer: solve four smaller versions of the identical problem, then combine. The combine here is simply 'hang them off a node'.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Is there a shortcut? Instead of scanning a region to check uniformity, could we build the children first and look at THEM?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Yes, and it is the neater version. Build all four children; if all four came back as leaves carrying the same value, collapse them into a single leaf and throw the children away.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Bottom-up instead of top-down. Same tree, and no separate scan to test uniformity.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One detail people trip on: the node's own value is meaningless when it is not a leaf. The problem lets you store anything there — so do not write logic that reads it.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Reading a non-leaf node's value, which the problem leaves unspecified. Also: the collapse only applies when all four children are leaves and share a value — four non-leaf children can never merge.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given a start gene, an end gene and a bank of valid genes, each 8 characters from {A, C, G, T}, return the fewest single-character mutations to get from start to end, where every intermediate gene must be in the bank. Return -1 if impossible.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Vegapunk's serum has to be transformed one letter at a time — and every single intermediate form has to be a gene the bank recognises. Anything else and it destabilises.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: This is a maze again, isn't it. It just doesn't look like one because there's no map.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Exactly. Genes are the places; a single-letter change to another valid gene is a corridor. Every mutation costs the same, so it is breadth-first search once more.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: But how do I find the neighbours of a gene? Compare it against everything in the bank and keep the ones differing by one letter?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is one way, and with a small bank it is perfectly reasonable. But there is a better one: generate the neighbours instead of searching for them. Eight positions, four letters — thirty-two candidates, and you simply ask the bank whether each exists.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Thirty-two lookups instead of scanning a bank of ten thousand. That scales much better as the bank grows.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: From the start gene, changing the last letter gives a gene the bank knows. One mutation.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: From there, changing the third letter reaches the target. Two mutations, and BFS guarantees there is no shorter route.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One rule that catches people: the END gene must itself be in the bank. It is an intermediate like any other as far as validity goes, and if it is absent the answer is minus one no matter how close it looks.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: And the START gene doesn't have to be in the bank, because you're already standing on it. That asymmetry is exactly the sort of thing I'd get wrong at two in the morning.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is why you read the constraints twice before you write a line. The search here is five lines; the reading is the hard part.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Forgetting that the end gene must appear in the bank, while the start gene need not. Also, mark genes visited on enqueue, and remember a mutation counts even when it lands on a gene you have already seen — you simply do not re-explore it.

452.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Balloons are given as [start, end] intervals along a horizontal line. An arrow shot straight up at a single x-coordinate bursts every balloon whose interval it passes through, including balloons that only touch at an endpoint. Find the minimum number of arrows needed to burst every balloon.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Behold! Four balloons strung along the wall, each spanning a range: 10-to-16, 2-to-8, 1-to-6, and 7-to-12. One arrow fired straight up at a single point bursts EVERY balloon whose range includes that point. What's the fewest arrows the great sniper Usopp needs to pop them all?

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: There are only four, but if there were hundreds, trying every possible arrow position sounds impossible!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: First, sort the balloons by where they END: 1–6, then 2–8, then 7–12, then 10–16. Now the rule is simple — always aim the next arrow at the END of the earliest still-unburst balloon. That one arrow is guaranteed to also burst every later balloon that starts before or at that point.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: First balloon, 1–6: no arrow fired yet. Fire one at x = 6, its end point!

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Next, 2–8: it starts at 2, which is at or before our arrow at 6. Already burst — no new arrow needed.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Next, 7–12: it starts at 7, which is PAST our arrow at 6. This one survived! Fire a second arrow at its end, x = 12.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Last, 10–16: it starts at 10, which is at or before our arrow at 12. Already burst by the same second arrow — no new arrow needed.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: All four balloons down, and it only took TWO arrows! The legendary sniper strikes again!

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: SHISHISHI! Usopp, that was actually really cool!

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Sort by where things end, not where they start. Fire only when forced to. Nothing fancier than that.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Sorting by START coordinate instead of END coordinate — that breaks the greedy guarantee, because the earliest-starting balloon might stretch out much farther than a balloon that starts later but ends sooner, causing the algorithm to under- or over-count arrows.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: You start with capital w and may complete at most k projects. Each project needs a minimum capital to start and pays a profit that is added to your capital. Maximise your final capital.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Big Mom is auctioning contracts. Each one needs a certain amount of Berries up front, and each pays out when it's done. We can take two — and every payout goes straight back into our purse for the next bid.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: So take the biggest payout first! Three Berries profit, obviously.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: We can't. That one needs one Berry to start and we're holding zero. The only contract we can afford right now is the one that needs nothing.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So there are two questions here, not one: which contracts can we afford, and among those, which pays best. Different questions, different structures.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Sort the contracts by what they REQUIRE. Then as our purse grows, we sweep a pointer forward and everything it passes has become affordable — permanently, because our purse never shrinks.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: And the affordable ones go into a max-heap by profit. Then choosing is just taking the top.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Purse is zero. Only the first contract is affordable, so it goes in the heap. Take it: purse becomes one.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Now with one Berry, BOTH remaining contracts become affordable. Both go into the heap — and the heap hands us the three, not the two.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Four Berries, in two contracts. Note that we never removed anything from the pool when we could not afford it — the pointer only moves forward, so each contract is considered exactly once.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: What if at some point nothing at all is affordable?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then stop. Our purse cannot grow without completing a contract, so if nothing is affordable now, nothing ever will be. Breaking out early is not an optimisation — it is the termination condition.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Greedily taking the largest profit without checking affordability, or re-sorting on every round. Also: if the heap is empty you must stop — the capital cannot grow, so no later round can succeed.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the root of a binary search tree, return the minimum absolute difference between the values of any two different nodes.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: Moria has stolen five shadows and hung them in his tree by weight. Two of them belong to the same person — and the only clue is that their weights are closer together than any other pair. Yohohoho, a grim little puzzle!

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Five shadows, so ten pairs. We could just measure every pair! ...though with five hundred shadows that's over a hundred thousand measurements, and I'd like to leave this island.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: We don't need every pair. This is a search tree — everything smaller hangs to the left, everything larger to the right. Which means if we walk it left, node, right, the shadows come out in sorted order.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Left-most first. One. Then its parent, two. Then two's right child, three. Then the root, four. Then six. One, two, three, four, six — perfectly ordered, and we never sorted anything.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: And in a sorted line, the closest pair must be NEIGHBOURS. If two shadows had something between them, that something would be closer to each of them than they are to each other.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So we only measure adjacent pairs. Nine gaps instead of ten pairs here — but on five hundred shadows, four hundred and ninety-nine gaps instead of a hundred and twenty-five thousand pairs.

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: One and two — a gap of one. Two and three — one again. Three and four — one. Four and six — two. The smallest gap is one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: And we never built the sorted list. We carry one number — the previous shadow visited — and compare it against the current one as the traversal passes through. Constant extra memory beyond the recursion itself.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Wait. What if I did the traversal wrong and went node, left, right instead? Then I'd get four, two, one, three, six — and comparing four with two would give me two, which isn't the answer at all!

clips.speaker: brook
clips.line: Precisely why the order matters more than the walking. In-order is the only traversal that turns a search tree into a sorted line. Get the order wrong and neighbours stop meaning anything. Yohohoho!

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Comparing the wrong pairs. Only in-order gives sorted output — pre-order or post-order neighbours are meaningless here. The other slip is initialising prev to 0 rather than to "nothing yet", which invents a phantom node at zero and can report a difference that does not exist.

637.title: Average of Levels in Binary Tree
637.epTitle: Weighing Each Floor of the Courthouse

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Given the root of a binary tree, return an array of the average value of the nodes on each level, from the top down.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: The courthouse has to be weighed floor by floor before they load the cannons. Not the whole building — each floor's average, separately.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: That's exactly the shape BFS hands you for free. You don't have to work out which floor anything is on — the queue already knows.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Snapshot the queue length. That is the number of rooms on this floor — the denominator. Then drain exactly that many, adding as you go. That is the numerator.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Floor one: one room, weighing three. Average three.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Floor two: two rooms, nine and twenty. Twenty-nine over two — fourteen and a half.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: Floor three: fifteen and seven. Twenty-two over two — eleven.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Depth-first would answer this too, but it would need a running sum and a count indexed by depth, carried through the recursion. Breadth-first hands you the level as a unit, because the level IS its unit of work.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Pick the traversal whose natural chunk matches the question's chunk. That's a rule I can actually remember.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: One thing worries me. These are courthouse ledgers — the values can be huge. If a floor has thousands of rooms, does the running total overflow?

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: In a fixed-width language, yes — sum with a wider type, or divide as you go. In Python integers grow, so it is safe, but knowing which of those two worlds you are in is exactly the sort of thing an interviewer is listening for.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Integer division. In languages where / truncates, the average of 9 and 20 becomes 14 rather than 14.5. Also watch the running sum's width on wide levels with large values.

909.title: Snakes and Ladders
909.epTitle: The Six Levels and the Chutes Between Them

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: On an n x n board numbered in boustrophedon order, each move rolls 1 to 6 forward. Some squares carry you instantly to another square. Return the fewest moves to reach the last square, or -1 if it cannot be reached.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Six levels of Impel Down, and the stairs between them don't run straight. Some cells have chutes that dump you two levels down; some have ladders that shoot you up. From any cell you can move one to six steps along the corridor.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: We need the FEWEST moves to reach Ace. Not any route — the shortest one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Then stop thinking about a board and start thinking about a graph. Every square is a place; a roll of one through six is six edges leaving it; a chute or ladder just means the edge lands somewhere other than where you counted to.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And every roll costs the same — one move. So all the edges weigh the same.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Which is exactly when breadth-first search is the shortest-path algorithm. It finishes an entire ring of squares reachable in one move before it touches anything needing two. So the first time we arrive anywhere, we have arrived by the shortest route.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: From square one, we can roll to squares two through seven. Square two has a ladder to fifteen, so rolling a one actually puts us on fifteen.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: Careful with the chute rule though. When a square carries you elsewhere, you take the destination and you do NOT then take that destination's own chute. One transport per landing.

clips.speaker: chopper
clips.line: And we mark a square as visited the moment we put it in the queue — not when we take it out.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: That is the difference between a working search and one that grinds. Six rolls per square means a square can be queued six times over before it is ever processed. Mark on entry and each square enters exactly once.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Four rings out, we touch the final square. Four moves. And if the queue empties without ever reaching it — then there's no way down at all, and the answer is minus one.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: The whole difficulty of this one is the board's numbering — it snakes back and forth, so turning a square number into a row and column takes a moment's care. Get that helper right on paper and the search itself is textbook.

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Chaining transports — if a ladder lands you on a snake, you do not take the snake. And marking visited on dequeue instead of enqueue, which lets a square be queued once per incoming roll.

918.title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
918.epTitle: The Ring That Has No End

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: Same as maximum subarray, except the array is circular: the run may wrap around from the end back to the beginning. Each element may still be used at most once.

clips.speaker: usopp
clips.line: Bad news. The Colosseum floor is a RING. After the last block, the gate opens straight back onto the first one. Zoro's run can wrap right around the far side.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Five, then minus three, then five. Walking it straight, my best is a single block: five. But if I finish on the last block and carry through onto the first — that's ten.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: So do we simulate the ring? Lay the blocks out twice and run the whole thing again? That works, but it doubles everything and we have to police the length so nobody fights the same block twice.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: There's a cleaner way. Look at what a wrapping run leaves BEHIND. It always leaves one unbroken block of rounds in the middle — the part he skipped.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: So a wrapping run is simply everything, minus that middle stretch. To make the run as large as possible, make the skipped stretch as SMALL as possible.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: Two runs of Kadane, then. One hunting the best stretch, one hunting the worst. Total is seven. The worst stretch is that lone minus three. Seven minus minus three is ten.

clips.speaker: nami
clips.line: Ten beats the straight-line answer of five. So the answer is the better of the two cases — no wrap, or wrap.

clips.speaker: robin
clips.line: One trap, and it is a nasty one. If every block is a loss, then the 'smallest middle stretch' is the entire ring — and total minus total is zero, which means fighting nothing at all.

clips.speaker: zoro
clips.line: And I'm not allowed to fight nothing. So when the straight-line best is already negative, that IS the answer — ignore the wrap entirely.

clips.speaker: luffy
clips.line: The ring has no end, so you take the whole thing and cut out the worst part! That's easier than running around twice!

clips.speaker: _narrator
clips.line: When every element is negative, total - minSum is 0 — the empty subarray — and it will beat the real answer. Guard it: if the straight-line maximum is negative, return that and never consider the wrap.

announcer.lose: Defeat. Study the debrief, then run it back.
